title: Why Warnock Didn’t Sleep on Mississippi
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts “I am here because I am tired of the South being overlooked or diminished in terms
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts “I am here because I am tired of the South being overlooked or diminished in terms of its electoral importance,” Senator Raphael Warnock told Mississippi Today back in October after stumping for Scott Colom
He’s the first Black Mississippian elected to the U.S

Senate since Reconstruction. “We lose elections by the margins of our disengagement,” Warnock said then. “Mississippi is a blue state; it just doesn’t know it yet.” Warnock, the pastor of Atlanta’s Ebenezer Baptist Church, was one of the few national Democrats who spent time in Mississippi this cycle
He raised hundreds of thousands of campaign dollars
Last week, when news outlets finally called the race in Mississippi, America woke up to the race everyone was “sleeping on,” as Warnock put it back in April

Democrats, who had ceded the South to Republicans for the past several decades, now believe that the political possibilities in the region are changing and have even further to go; few Democrats on the national stage believe that as much as Warnock

For this week’s episode of Radio Atlantic , I spoke with Warnock at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta about the uptick in turnout in the 2026 midterms, how to protect the vote in future elections, and what his agenda looks like in the years to come
The following is a transcript of the episode: Senator Raphael Warnock: You have to compromise in politics
But I’m not going to compromise my integrity, just to maintain an office. [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic
I’m Adam Harris, and today: a conversation with Senator Raphael Warnock about voting rights, the South, and what he wants to get done in the next Congress
On January 5, 2021, Warnock became the first Black senator in Georgia’s history
And to Warnock, both events represent America

Those dates—January 5 and January 6—represent the promise and the violence of its history And to him, when Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi’s Senate race, Warnock believed it was another promising moment
Few people – including national Democrats – believed Colom’s win was possible, but Warnock did
He was one of the few who supported him early and often
He says it’s because he believes a new South is a real possibility

On Thursday evening, at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, I sat down with Senator Warnock to talk about what needs to be done to protect voting rights, what political success looks like for Democrats, and how to hold the tension that America is both January 5 and January 6
Here’s our conversation: Adam Harris: Senator, it’s great to be with you this evening
Harris: Yeah, absolutely, and thank you all for joining us
I’ve been looking forward to this conversation, particularly as we’ve seen the South change a bit over the last couple of days
For a long time, political possibility in the South has been sort of limited by both discrimination and also sort of lack of imagination
In 2021, you became Georgia’s first Black senator
What does Scott Colom’s win in Mississippi, what do these wins in Georgia tell us about political possibility in the South? Warnock: What a remarkable moment in American history
And I’m just honored and deeply humbled to be a small part of it
I’m so happy for the people of Mississippi
But let’s be clear: Mississippi did an incredible thing for the whole country
They nudged us a little closer to our ideals
And Scott Colom ran an incredibly innovative, creative, and scrappy campaign because he had very little resources
But I wanna be clear, because sometimes on the other side of these victories, we forget what it costs
This didn’t roll in on the wheels of inevitability
I know what it’s like for people to believe, for people to think you can’t do it
And it always looks impossible until it’s done
Cycle after cycle, we kept telling folks, It can happen in Georgia , and they didn’t believe us
Because it’s easy to forget now that I’m here
A Black senator and a Jewish senator in one fell swoop
But I don’t want you to miss this: The people of Mississippi did an amazing thing

I know you were wondering, Well, when are they gonna finish counting all those ballots? But here’s the question you ought to ask yourself: Why is that the case? So there were provisional ballots, and why were there provisional ballots? Because people had been purged from the roll
Georgia, by the way, was quite good at that
They purged 500,000 voters one Saturday night here in Georgia
And so people’s names had been purged from the rolls, and so that’s why they had to cast a provisional ballot

title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
excerpt: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado tou
body: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday
The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h)
There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95

Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones
A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter)
Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday
Such storms are common at this time of year
Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones

title: The Dangerous Idea Rubio and Hegseth Are Endorsing
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

When Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was reprimanded by a sentinel last week for a lack of decorum at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, his response was unusually gracious: He promptly awarded the sentinel the Joint Service Commendation Medal
Perhaps Hegseth’s conciliatory response was not because he recognized he’d violated the sanctity of the location , but because he’d been yelled at by one authority he recognizes: a man with a gun
This thought occurred to me over the weekend, when Hegseth posted a clip of Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaking at a Federalist Society conference Friday evening
Rubio praised President Trump’s sanctions earlier this year on the International Criminal Court
So far, so normal: The right has long despised the ICC, arguing that it violates American sovereignty and could be used as a foreign-policy weapon by U.S. adversaries

Rubio said that if the ICC tried to exercise jurisdiction over Americans, “our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general, Pompey, when he said to those who were trying to invoke their cities’ charters against his legions
He said, ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’” This is an odd thing to say to a room full of lawyers, and it was met with some awkward chuckles
Only once Rubio declared Pompey’s statement as “not politically correct” did he win applause

But Hegseth was apparently taken with the quote and reposted it, writing , “Stop quoting laws to MEN WITH SWORDS.” Rubio and Hegseth are expressing a core view of the second Trump administration: that might makes right and rules are for sissies

In January, now–White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller explained the American quasi-colonization of Venezuela this way. “We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world,” he said, “that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power

These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.” (No wonder that the United States—with Rubio acting as viceroy—has signaled that it prefers rule by the Nicolás Maduro protégé Delcy Rodríguez to María Corina Machado’s attempts to restore democracy in the country.) Trump has shown that he prefers the performative machismo of Vladimir Putin’s Russian military to Ukraine’s legal and moral claim on its land, and he has mused publicly about actions against Iran that would be war crimes
The Trumpist fidelity to this idea is particularly true with regard to international law, but it extends to a consistent disregard for the laws of the United States as well

At the Pentagon, Hegseth has raged against rules of engagement for the military and loosened them for the war in Iran, which may be one reason that the U.S. bombed an elementary school in Iran early in the conflict. (Superior American military might has not prevailed in Iran so far, either.) The military has also killed almost 250 people in extrajudicial and likely illegal strikes on boats that American officials allege are carrying drugs

The epithet un-American is overused, but in this case, it is literally true. “The very purpose of the American founding was to ensure that force would always be subject to law, which would itself flow from natural right and popular consent,” John R

Puri writes in National Review . “That is why one of the Founders’ great innovations was to place the new U.S. armed forces under strict civilian control.” One specific complaint in the Declaration of Independence was that King George III had “affected to render the Military independent of and superior to the Civil power.” By contrast, John Adams wrote that a republic was a government “of Laws, and not of Men,” a stipulation that very much includes men with swords who might try to supersede law

Hegseth is himself now a lawless man with (metaphorical) swords, and in his enthusiastic endorsement of Rubio’s remark, we may find insight into both why Hegseth joined the Army out of college and why his career languished
Maybe he thought joining the military was a ticket to cracking heads without restriction
Instead, he found a careful, disciplined, and rule-abiding force, and he never advanced very far

Cohen has written , “The Army, unlike Princeton and Harvard, knew a petulant, insecure mediocrity when it saw one.” Hegseth eventually left the National Guard when he was sidelined over concerns about extremism
As secretary, he has gone about destroying the institution that spurned him, as well as working to ensure that the people bearing swords are almost entirely men
As for Rubio, he has recently become a fount of classical references , perhaps under the influence of white-nationalist ideas circulating at the State Department
But mouthing these words is different from understanding what they mean

As a young commander during a Roman civil war in the 80s B.C.E., Pompey earned the nickname adulescentulus carnifex —“teenage butcher.” When residents of the Sicilian city of Messana resisted his authority, citing ancient Roman law, he uttered the quotation that Rubio cites
The American Founders—and indeed most Americans throughout history—would have seen themselves in the citizens of Messana, not the ruthless general
He enjoyed years of political and military success during a period when republican rule was teetering, eventually becoming part of a ruling triumvirate with Julius Caesar and Marcus Licinius Crassus
But he eventually fell out with Caesar, resulting in another civil war
Pompey fled Rome but was killed and beheaded in Egypt
Nor, more important, did Pompey’s era end well for the Roman Republic
When the long-running political crisis that spawned both civil wars was over, the republic was dead, and Rome was ruled by an emperor
It is possible—even probable—that the Trump figures quoting Pompey do not know this history
But understanding it is not necessary to grasp why Pompey’s words are nothing to emulate, nor to predict what will happen to a republic that allows such leaders to reach and maintain power

title: The Real Reason Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond
excerpt: Picking a new James Bond has long followed a tried-and-tested formula: Don’t go too famous
body: Picking a new James Bond has long followed a tried-and-tested formula: Don’t go too famous
The secret agent has nearly always been played by an up-and-coming, well-regarded talent who looks good in a tux

So for years, as the debate has dragged on over who would replace Daniel Craig in the role, dozens of names along those lines have bubbled up; these most recently included Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor
Some possible candidates aged out of the role while waiting for it to open up, in the same way that potential popes find themselves hitting retirement age before their chance at the papacy arrives

But the final choice for the new Bond, Robert Pattinson, completely defies that established logic: By casting someone who’s already globally popular, the franchise is somehow taking the risky version of a typically very safe bet

Pattinson makes plenty of sense on paper as Bond: He’s about the right age (he turned 40 this year) and the right height, at 6 foot 1; he’s debonair and British in all the appreciable ways; he wears a suit better than anyone. (His work in Tenet is one of the best-tailored performances of all time.) But unlike most of his predecessors, he’s also one of the most famous A-listers working today
He’s featured in multiple hit franchises and is also the current occupant of another iconic role, Batman
And because the Bond franchise is in the hands of new ownership for the first time in decades, the old formulas clearly no longer apply
Pattinson’s career started out traditionally enough

He first broke out as a teenager playing Cedric Diggory in the fourth Harry Potter movie before becoming a superstar in his 20s thanks to the Twilight movies—dark romantic fantasies aimed at young adults that were largely dismissed or mocked by critics upon release
But the actor has harnessed his early celebrity to create a constantly shifting and unique persona as a performer

He’s worked with numerous acclaimed directors across genres, Christopher Nolan, David Cronenberg, James Gray, Claire Denis, the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers, Bong Joon Ho, and Lynne Ramsay among them

When he’s appeared in more conventional blockbusters, he’s put a weird imprimatur on them, as with his emo version of Batman; in December, he’s popping up in Dune: Part Three as an eyebrow-less, shapeshifting villain. [ Read: The James Bond trap ] In a way, playing Bond seems almost too normal for Pattinson
He certainly looks the part in the one promo image that Amazon dropped; he’s a handsome Brit with a chiseled jaw who’s clad in a tux and toting a gun, as per usual for the MI6 super-spy
But one hopes he’ll be able to bring a stranger energy to the role than the Bonds before him
Craig played the character in five movies, culminating in 2021’s No Time to Die ; his take was flinty and frightening, a swerve from Pierce Brosnan’s suave demeanor

Pattinson will likely come across as even more sophisticated—he’s taller and more willowy than Craig, and more traditionally “posh.” And the DC cinematic universe’s recent behind-the-scenes shake-up probably helped Pattinson commit to the franchise, considering that his future as Batman now seems murky

But I hope there’s room in his schedule to maintain the wacky streak he’s shown in movies such as last year’s Mickey 17 , as well as the more alien, lizard-like quality that made his performance in The Batman , along with this year’s The Odyssey and Primetime , so compelling
In previous eras, one would be foolish to hope for that sort of originality
The Bond property had long been a rarity in Hollywood: It was essentially run as a tightly controlled family business
Eon Productions, which was led by the producers Michael G
Wilson and Barbara Broccoli, managed the franchise that they’d inherited from their father; creatively, the buck stopped with them
They relied on a core group of collaborators who knew what a Bond movie should look and feel like, extending beyond whoever was playing the role
That consistency was helpful in building the brand, but it sometimes felt stultifying
Now that Amazon owns Bond outright, the company is making choices that suggest that a more prestigious take on the character is en route
This is not to diss some of the prior Bond films’ directors
Sam Mendes, who made two of the Craig movies, is an Oscar winner—yet he’d made a few flops before he got the gig
Directors such as Cary Fukunaga, Marc Forster, Martin Campbell, and Lee Tamahori were all fairly reliable picks with some large-canvas action experience
But the next installment’s director, Denis Villeneuve, is a glitzy choice: He’s highly regarded by critics and is coming off a giant franchise success of his own with Dune
Among action filmmakers, only Nolan is a bigger name right now (and he was reportedly counted out for the job because he’d require the right to final cut—i.e., total creative control)
Amazon’s decision to spare no expense or risk for handling the biggest name-brand property it owns seems obvious
For all the creative ups and downs of the Craig era, the actor was a beloved Bond for 15 years; his memory will be difficult to displace
Rather than roll the dice on a (relative) unknown in search of something new and different, the brand’s new owners are opting for A-list quality
Pattinson is not an outside-the-box choice for Bond
Somehow, he still feels like a total surprise.

title: Sorry, Robert Pattinson Is Not James Bond
excerpt: Robert Pattinson is, I’m sure, a fine actor
body: Robert Pattinson is, I’m sure, a fine actor
I cannot vouch for this because I have not seen him in movies I’ve liked
Granted, I have not seen his entire body of work; I was already in my 40s when he landed his big role as a vampire in Twilight , a movie that was not exactly aimed at my demographic
I am a fan of superhero movies, and he was, in my view, a terrible Batman: He made Bruce Wayne into a dull cop in a costume
Still, he seems to be working a lot, so someone out there likes him
Amazon MGM Studios, which now owns the movie franchise, announced today that he’ll take over the role
Yet Pattinson lacks the manly gravitas, the physicality, the wit, to play the world’s most dangerous spy
As a kid, I saw the Sean Connery movies only on television
I was 13 when I saw my first Bond film on a big screen: Live and Let Die , starring Roger Moore
It was a revelation. (I was old enough to start getting the jokes about sex, for one thing.) I then devoured, in proper sequence, all the Ian Fleming novels that inspired the movies
When I visited London as a teen in 1975, I didn’t care about seeing Parliament or the crown jewels
I wanted to be Moore—hey, he was the only movie Bond working at the time—and wander the streets once walked by the British spy who always saved the world and got the girl
I know the voice, mannerisms, and quips of every cinematic Bond
I also know what Fleming’s Bond looks and sounds like

According to Fleming, he was based on the 1940s bandleader Hoagy Carmichael, if that makes any sense to you, and I even know where Bond’s boss, M, has his office and his favorite club. (I also know his full name: Miles Messervy
You’re welcome.) I know what Bond’s maid, May, makes him every day for breakfast

And Robert Pattinson, you are no James Bond. [ From the March 2024 issue: The James Bond trap ] Bond does not need to be a hairy bruiser; in the movies he loses plenty of fights, and in the books he routinely gets beaten to a pulp and ends up in the enemy’s clutches
Connery was perhaps the most macho of the Bonds, whereas Moore was the most dainty
All of them, however, were charismatic rogues, mature adults who could shoot, fight, drink, and—well, other things

They enjoyed every martini and they made a play for every shapely woman who crossed their path. (Bond is suave and a hero, but he’s also a boozy, sexist boor.) Can Pattinson carry the legacy of any of his predecessors? Aficionados will disagree on who made the best Bond, but each actor had a niche

Connery was a product of the Cold War and the swinging ’60s. (He came back to play Bond once in 1971, Diamonds Are Forever , a misfire that included fitting him with a bad toupee; he made one more mediocre Bond film in 1983 with a different production company as a one-off outside the “canonical” Bond series.) A temporary replacement Bond, an Australian named George Lazenby, did a fine job in one movie, and then blew his career by walking away from the character

Moore, like the rest of us, did his best to make his way through the silly 1970s, but I think he is underappreciated: His 007 grimly faced down Christopher Lee in The Man With the Golden Gun and dispatched not one but two genocidal freaks bent on planetary destruction: a web-fingered weirdo in The Spy Who Loved Me and a eugenics-obsessed, space-industry billionaire—a plot clearly ahead of its time—in Moonraker
Moore was a decent Bond, but stayed with the role too long
In 1985, the 57-year-old Moore had a love scene with 36-year-old Grace Jones in A View to a Kill

Timothy Dalton, another underappreciated Bond, was an accomplished Shakespearean actor who moved into the role easily, and brought a combination of Connery’s violent physicality and Moore’s caddish humor. (Watch the pre-credits sequence of The Living Daylights , which is one of the best cold opens in the entire series.) Producers had begun looking at the next Bond, Pierce Brosnan, when he was still playing the TV detective Remington Steele and was too young and callow to play a spy who was licensed to kill
But as he matured, he was an obvious choice to play Bond perhaps like no actor since Connery

Brosnan took Bond into the new, post–Cold War world with style, but also with murderous determination: In GoldenEye , one of the best Bond movies, Brosnan looks directly into his best friend’s face and then drops him to his death
All of these men as Bond exuded a kind of energetic and masculine combination of professionalism and uncontrollable individuality
In the books, 007 is a complex character who soldiers on because it’s his job

But all of that anguish would make for a drab series of movies, and to their credit, Connery, Lazenby, Moore, Brosnan, and even the dour Dalton manage to look they’re having fun—at least when they’re not about to be cut in half by lasers or strangled by a python
Here I will aggravate a lot of Bond fans: I think the series went off the rails with the casting of Daniel Craig and a drastic change in the 007 scripts
Instead of taking on supervillains, Bond tussled with terrorists and financiers, all while thinking and talking way too much about his psyche
Craig, another fine actor, was too brutish, and the scripts make plain that the job did, in fact, get to him

Craig’s Bond dressed well enough, but he always seemed uncomfortable in his suits: He’s a brawler with deep, complicated feelings, and one thing the cinematic James Bond does not need is a lot of feelings

The Craig scripts became like therapy sessions: When the big reveal came in the Craig movie Spectre— that the sadistic, megalomaniacal genius Ernst Blofeld was actually just a little boy with hurt feelings whose dad liked Jimmy Bond better when they were kids—I nearly walked out of the theater. (And by the way, what an utter waste of Christoph Waltz, who was born to play Blofeld.) By settling on Pattinson, who is even more angsty than Craig, the producers seem intent on continuing the decline

At least in the performances I’ve seen, Pattinson is sensitive ; he broods ; he’s conflicted ; he has messy hair; he has deep, watery eyes; he— He’s a walking young-Millennial stereotype, is what I’m saying. [ Read: Leave James Bond alone ] He doesn’t appear old or tough or coldly professional enough to be Bond
Think of this: Connery was 31 when he filmed Dr
Dalton was 41 when he strapped on his Walther PPK
Craig was 37 when he sat at the card table in Casino Royale

Pattinson is 40—and yet all of these guys look self-assured and old enough to play Pattinson’s father, not his colleague. (Even Brosnan seems like a tougher old brother, not a fellow Double-O.) Having most recently watched Pattinson mumble and anguish his way through The Batman , I cannot imagine him driving a Soviet tank through the streets of Russia, lecturing M on the finer points of blending cognac, or gently pushing the bad guy out of a space station’s airlock with an invitation to “take a giant step for mankind.” Perhaps the next film will do wonders; Moore, for one, was usually better when the scripts stuck to action instead of cheap comedy

title: Are You Sure the Problem Is Pajamas, Sean Duffy?
excerpt: If it isn’t my old nemesis, Sean Duffy, in the news again
body: If it isn’t my old nemesis, Sean Duffy, in the news again

Did something happen at the airports, Sean? Was it very bad? Would you go so far as to describe it as a serious problem? Worse, say, than people dressing casually at the airport, perhaps even in pajamas ? Because I would
Now, I’m only a breathable, comfortable nighttime garment, but I think it is good when the planes aren’t afraid to go up and then come down again
To me, that is the most important thing that happens at an airport
Call me old-fashioned, but I think the planes should get to leave the ground
That’s just a superstition I have! A total ground stop
Planes everywhere, stuck on the tarmacs; spoonfuls of mashed bananas, unable to reach reluctant toddlers’ mouths
For hours, you say? Now, that sounds like a real airport problem
It would be a shame if you had alienated your old friend Travel Pajamas in a situation like this
I do not mean to question how much you know about aviation
I don’t know what your job is! Something where you get to appear on television a lot and nothing is your fault? In times of trouble, Mr
Rogers always told us to look for the helpers
Pajamas swathed travel-weary limbs in a soft fabric embrace
Where were you? Saying on CNN that you “take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations”? That doesn’t sound like taking responsibility
I am cozy with everyone, not just the industry I am meant to regulate

The fact that your reality-TV show (no, not The Real World , the other one) was called The Great American Road Trip and not Touring America Safely via Uninterrupted Air Travel should perhaps have signaled to us that all was not well
And now I am sure you will find someone to blame

Blame AI! Blame “systems”! Blame the “patriot” who installed the router! Say you don’t know what the problem was, but you will need $50 billion to fix it! That won’t fly, not unlike every plane on Friday night
I would suggest that this incident was someone’s chickens coming home to roost—or they would have been coming home to roost if there weren’t a ground stop
This was a case of chickens circling above the airport hoping for permission to land, then being stuck on the tarmac for hours
When you slandered me, all those months ago, and blamed me for everything that was wrong with air travel, I held my peace
But now I am asking respectfully (I know respect means a lot to you) for my apology
Was the problem really that people were not dressing like it was 50 years ago, Sean? Was that really the problem? Thank you for your time
Good day! I will see you this evening, when I will do my best to make you as happy and comfortable as you have failed to make me

title: The Rise of the Fusion Democrat
excerpt: Y ou could use practically any synonym for big to describe this month’s Democratic wins
body: Y ou could use practically any synonym for big to describe this month’s Democratic wins
For the first time in 145 years, Mississippi will have a Black senator
Roughly three-quarters of the nation’s population will now be led by Democratic governors
In the House, the Democrats expect a roomy 80-plus-seat margin over Republicans
Latinos? Young men? Working-class white people? On Election Day, they all moved left
Moderates would like to take credit for this turn in the party’s fortunes, especially in red states
This irks progressives, who point out that many of the winners actually sounded a lot like Bernie Sanders
But a few brave contrarians have also waded into these muddy waters
They argue that there is a different way to look at the results, one that might quell the Democrats’ infighting
Their explanation involves a word that one might expect to see in the context of, say, a corn tortilla stuffed with bulgogi: fusion
Democrats won this year, the progressive pollster Adam Carlson told me, by taking “a little from everyone.” The internecine fights over labels might seem petty
But for Democrats, these squabbles are crucial

The lessons that the party learns from this election will inform not only how its politicians govern, but also how they behave in the 2028 election cycle, which, if you haven’t heard, is already in full swing
M ost Americans showed up to the polls last week fueled by pent-up anger and profound weariness, polling shows
They voted against President Trump and Republican leadership, rather than affirmatively for a bold and beautiful Democratic vision

The political challenge for Democrats now is how to interpret the results: whether the campaigns they ran this cycle should be replicated in 2028—and from which faction of the party the presidential candidates should take their cues
The problem is that these factions are at war, and have been for a long while
Progressives say that the mandate belongs to them

They point to the fact that many successful candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, ran on ending corporate corruption and taxing the heck out of America’s billionaires
These winning Democrats, they argue, campaigned using the kind of “fighting oligarchy” message popularized by Sanders and Senator Elizabeth Warren

More data: The Congressional Progressive Caucus will add at least 25 new members, bringing its record-high membership to more than 105; the number of lawmakers who identify as democratic socialists will quadruple, from two to eight. “If those who call themselves moderate want to slap their label on candidates who campaigned on our issues, then cool—we’ve won the battle for the heart, soul, and future direction of the party,” Adam Green, a co-founder of the Progressive Change Institute, said when the group released its postelection analysis
Moderates, unfortunately for Green, do want to slap their label on those candidates
They point out that economic populism is a long-standing principle of the Democratic Party, not a concept owned by progressives
They also note that the Democrats who flipped Republican Senate seats found ways to signal their independence from progressive orthodoxy
In Texas, for example, Talarico embraced the oil industry
In Iowa, Josh Turek campaigned on border security, and opposed allowing transgender women to play in women’s sports

None of the successful red-state Senate Democrats endorsed Medicare for All. “The lesson from this cycle is unequivocal: high-quality Democrats in the middle were the majority makers in 2026—and they are the model for 2028,” reads one analysis from the centrist think tank Third Way

The Blue Dog Coalition, a tiny House caucus of moderate Democrats, will more than double next year, expanding to at least 22 members. [ Read: The GOP’s culture-war Hail Mary ] But a third group of Democrats is attempting to make peace between the factions
These Democrats believe that their candidates won because they managed to combine some of the best ideas from both camps—baking a moderate cake and slathering it with a fluffy layer of progressivism

What if—and hear them out—Democrats can have it all? “This election points toward a new liberal fusionism, candidates who combine leftist economic populism with centrist pragmatism,” Rotimi Adeoye, a member of the New York Times editorial board, wrote on X on November 4

He pronounced factional fighting, a feature of today’s Democratic Party, to be “old news, beltway chatter.” Some of the freshman lawmakers are already showing what fusion might look like in practical terms
Sam Forstag, a former smokejumper from Montana, for example, plans to join both the Blue Dogs and the Congressional Progressive Caucus
Former President Ronald Reagan was big on the concept, which was developed by the political philosopher Frank Meyer and promoted by the National Review editor William F
For Republicans, fusion meant blending traditional social conservatism with free-market libertarianism

For Democrats, it looks more like pairing socially moderate positions (don’t let transgender girls play girls’ sports; protect the border) with progressive economic ones (raise the minimum wage; tax the rich)

Proponents of fusionism love Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who talked nonstop about political and corporate corruption during his campaign for reelection, while simultaneously opposing several progressive priorities, such as Medicare for All, abolishing ICE , and expanding the Supreme Court

Talarico, too: The Texas state lawmaker repeated the line that the “only minority destroying America is the billionaires” but also criticized former President Biden for failing to secure the border, and moderated his position on the inclusion of trans kids in sports. [ Read: Jon Ossoff is doing something different ] Carlson, the pollster, believes that the combine-and-stir formulation can work well for Democrats

He’s listed a few priorities from the winning 2026 campaigns that he hopes become part of the blueprint for the national party: rooting out corruption, naming billionaires as the enemy, showing empathy on transgender issues, reclaiming patriotism, securing the border, and regulating AI companies. (Representative Sarah McBride of Delaware also appears to be a Fusion Head: “Co-sign
Spot on,” she responded to Carlson.) Other Democrats prefer to use different language

Adam Jentleson refers to this kind of mix-and-match thinking as “heterodox.” His think tank, Searchlight Institute, argues that to win a supermajority again in Congress, Democrats should not rigidly adhere to a set of positions simply because they’re on the party platform

title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers

But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world
These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies

Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech)

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created
They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.  But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI

New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.  On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated
China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead
It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips
DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position

He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China
It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him
The new findings lower Huang’s chances further
What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion

Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.  But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter

The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good
The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers
That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit

title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
excerpt: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them
body: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them
One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t
No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors
For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection
Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses
Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment
We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe
But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built
We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do
We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach
In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit
But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions

One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry
And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside
Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision
Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior
With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment
Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact
Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed
The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance
Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs
The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI

Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful
Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades

For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations
But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act
The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event
Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk

But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest
Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture

The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark
The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted
It means trust needs a different architecture
Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable
An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription
An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds
An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter

Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution

title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
excerpt: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments
body: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments
Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate

Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes
The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows

For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing

Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability

Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says
Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus

Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit
Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers
Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets

For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys

Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace
This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys
Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate

But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds
It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift
Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit
It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used
Two words for you: conscious configuration
My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy
Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us
Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys
Thanks for inviting for the conversation today
We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation
Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example
When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack? Thorsten: Yeah

Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise
And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation
This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale
At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed
For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale
And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization

The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle
And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes
Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support

And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well? Satinder: Absolutely, Megan
And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI

<p>World leaders are seeing their countries suffer from <a href="https://wmo.int/resources/publication-series/state-of-climate-update-cop/state-of-climate-update-cop31">intensifying storms and heat fueled by climate change</a> and from one of the <a href="https://www.weforum.org/stories/energy-transition/world-facing-biggest-ever-energy-crisis-and-more-top-energy-stories">worst global energy crises</a> in history. A U.N. report found that global warming will <a href="https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/limiting-overshoot-navigating-exceedance-15degc-and-pathways-towards-return">overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius</a> (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the level countries agreed a decade ago to try to avoid because of the growing risk of dangerous climate change.</p>

<p>The Middle East conflict has <a href="https://www.iea.org/topics/the-middle-east-and-global-energy-markets">intensified oil and gas price and supply volatility</a>, pushing economies to the brink as energy and food prices spike and energy security falters.</p>

<p>Countries that rely on imported fossil fuels for their energy sources have borne the brunt of the energy crisis. Those doubling down on renewable energy are weathering the crisis better.</p>

<p>In Pakistan, for example, the rapid expansion of solar power over the past six years helped the country avoid <a href="https://www.secureenergyproject.org/post/the-hedge-that-paid-off-how-pakistan-s-solar-boom-is-shielding-it-from-the-hormuz-crisis">more than US$12 billion</a> in fossil fuel imports before the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran began in February 2026. One forecast suggests solar could save the country <a href="https://www.secureenergyproject.org/post/the-hedge-that-paid-off-how-pakistan-s-solar-boom-is-shielding-it-from-the-hormuz-crisis">more than $6 billion more</a> by the end of the year. Spain, which relies less on natural gas and <a href="https://www.iea.org/countries/spain/energy-mix">more on solar energy for electricity</a> than most European countries, <a href="https://ember-energy.org/latest-insights/latest-energy-shock-reminds-europe-of-its-risky-gas-reliance/">kept electricity prices lower</a> and avoided the worst of the gas-driven spikes seen in more exposed systems such as Italy’s.</p>

<p>In formal negotiations and in meetings around the <a href="https://www.climatechampions.net/our-work/action-agenda/">U.N.’s broader Global Climate Action Agenda</a>, countries are working on ways to accelerate the use of clean energy and to provide poorer countries with the resources to adapt to climate change and expand clean energy.</p>

<p>I have been following international climate negotiations for years as a former special climate envoy for Germany and <a href="https://www.climatepolicylab.org/jennifer-morgan">senior fellow</a> at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. In 2026, after two years of the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/27/climate/trump-international-pressure-climate-oil.html">Trump administration’s pressure</a> to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/06/climate/trump-climate-international-bullying.html">get countries to abandon efforts to slow climate change</a>, I’m seeing rising concern among leaders about the costs of fossil fuels on economies and people’s lives.</p>

<h2>The electrification solution</h2>

<p>A step in transitioning away from fossil fuels is shifting to electrification powered by clean energy. The co-presidents of COP31, from Turkey and Australia, have proposed a global target of <a href="https://cop31.tr/action-plan/clean-energy">35% of all energy use coming from electricity by 2035</a> – including for transportation and industry – and they are working to persuade other countries to sign on.</p>

<p><iframe id="fWXMs" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/fWXMs/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Renewable energy is the fastest growth source of electricity globally, now on par with coal for the amount used globally."></iframe></p>

<p>Hitting that 35% mark could save fossil-fuel-importing countries <a href="https://www.iea.org/files/435d1d9e-2814-44a2-b059-e080987e3c79/Electrification.pdf">$400 billion a year</a>, according to the International Energy Agency. In consumer terms, $100 spent on electricity powers a car up to <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/electrification">three times farther</a> than $100 of gasoline, based on global averages. Reaching the goal could slash energy emissions across transportation, buildings and industry by <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/electrification">up to 55% by 2035</a>.</p>

<p>However, the source of electrification matters. Forecasts from the International Renewable Energy Agency show that at least <a href="https://www.irena.org/electrification">78% of the electricity</a> powering the world must come from renewable energy sources to keep global warming under the 1.5 C limit. Electrification delivers for both the climate and energy security if it runs on clean power instead of energy from oil, gas and coal. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Getting the world to that point will require addressing some key barriers: the cost of infrastructure needed to deliver clean energy and the need for policies to encourage the changes. </p>

<p>Beyond the formal negotiations, countries are discussing multiple initiatives to provide <a href="https://greengridsinitiative.net/news/technical-assistance-hub-launched-at-cop31-to-accelerate-modernisation-of-electricity-grids">technical support to one another</a>, as countries develop power grids that can manage the variability of solar and wind power, and <a href="https://www.electrifynow.world/news-and-resources/electrify-now-finance-coalition-launched-at-cop31">financial help</a> to countries that need it. </p>

<h2>Voters show their frustration with fossil fuels</h2>

<p>The high financial and environmental costs of fossil fuels have been reshaping global politics. Voters came out in big numbers over the past few months to elect leaders who support clean, affordable energy solutions.</p>

<p>The world saw this notably with the <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/11/brazil-election-cop-un-climate-lula-01161268">reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva</a> and the <a href="https://theconversation.com/epic-blue-wave-helps-democrats-take-congress-in-overwhelming-rebuke-to-president-trump-295830">biggest Democratic congressional victory</a> in the United States in over three decades.</p>

<p>Lula, in his first international trip after winning his fourth term, <a href="https://cop30.br/en/news-about-cop30/president-lula-brings-the-legacy-of-belem-to-cop31-urging-world-leaders-to-restore-climate-action-to-the-global-agenda">called on the COP31 presidents</a> to carry forward Brazil’s work as host of COP30 on a <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-battle-over-a-global-energy-transition-is-on-between-petro-states-and-electro-states-heres-what-to-watch-for-in-2026-272205">transition away from fossil fuels</a>. He announced that Brazil will <a href="https://theclimatewatch.com/lula-offers-to-host-future-fossil-fuel-transition-conference-in-brazil/">host a future conference</a> on the fossil fuel transition, following the first in Colombia in April 2026 and a second planned in 2027 in the island nation of Tuvalu.</p>

<p>Brazil has clearly emerged as a climate superpower in Antalya. With its <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/deforestation-brazils-amazon-falls-lowest-record-202526-2026-10-16/">greatest one-year reduction in deforestation</a> and its leadership in producing three plans, known as road maps, to help the world transition away from fossil fuels, end deforestation and <a href="https://cop30.br/en">provide the $1.3 trillion</a> in financing needed for developing countries, Brazil has demonstrated it understands the urgency of the climate crisis.</p>

<p>We will see whether the co-presidents of COP31 will answer the calls from Lula and <a href="https://webtv.un.org/en/asset/k13/k137pno7q4">U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres</a> to support these road maps becoming formal guidance for all countries.</p>

<h2>The Americans at COP31</h2>

<p>California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a delegation of <a href="https://www.seecinstitute.org/press/press-release-with-a-new-congress-on-the-horizon-18-us-lawmakers-arrive-at-cop31-to-signal-americas-return-to-sensible-climate-policynbsp">18 members of the U.S. House of Representatives</a> also came to COP31 to signal the presence of American leadership on future climate policy. President Donald Trump has <a href="https://theconversation.com/damn-the-torpedoes-trump-ditches-a-crucial-climate-treaty-in-latest-move-to-dismantle-americas-climate-protections-273148">pulled the U.S. out</a> of the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/12/trump-un-climate-treaty-unfccc">dozens of other international organizations and treaties</a>. The U.S. did not send a formal delegation to the climate talks.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As former U.S. climate envoy John Kerry <a href="https://transcripts.un.org/en/asset/k1b/k1brkp0hqo">said in Antalya</a>, “Americans did vote for clean, affordable energy, and they also voted for clean governance.”</p>

<p>The international community will be watching to see whether the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress can help safeguard U.S. climate science after the <a href="https://thebulletin.org/premium/2026-11/cuts-evictions-and-job-losses-a-view-from-the-trenches-of-climate-science-in-2026/">Trump administration’s extensive funding cuts</a>, and whether it will restore critical <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/ajil.2025.10112">funding to international efforts</a> dealing with climate change.</p>

<h2>What success looks like</h2>

<p>At COP31, the shift in the real-world politics of energy has dominated several events and the formal negotiations. But the countries <a href="https://houseofsaud.com/saudi-cop31-fossil-fuel-roadmap-nov12/">that are likely to lose</a> from such a transition are also working diligently to <a href="https://theconversation.com/5-ways-countries-stymie-climate-negotiations-without-actually-saying-no-295589">slow this transition</a>. On the opening day, a coalition of oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia announced it <a href="https://enb.iisd.org/antalya-un-climate-change-conference-cop31-daily-report-9nov2026">opposed any mention of Brazil’s road map</a> away from fossil fuels in the official COP31 agreement.  </p>

<p>For COP31 to be a success, the diplomatic process must demonstrate that it can catch up to the real economy and meet this moment of energy and climate crisis. I believe the summit’s final agreement should accelerate the electrification of infrastructure around the world and, at the same time, drive the transition away from fossil fuels in order to protect global security, economic stability and everyday citizens.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296682/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>New England’s first Bible, published in an Indigenous language, had one aim: Converting Native Americans</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771978/original/file-20261114-64-g3x0q4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=11%2C0%2C2310%2C1540&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The &#39;Eliot&#39; Bible, published in 1663, was the result of collaboration between a Puritan minister and a Montauk interpreter.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Index_and_Genesis_in_John_Eliot%27s_Bible.jpg">Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In 1663, colonial printers in New England produced a translation of the Bible into Wampanoag, <a href="https://www.wlrp.org/">an Algonquian language</a> <a href="https://www.si.edu/newsdesk/releases/smithsonian-researcher-discovers-new-native-american-languages-central-massachusetts">spoken in southern New England</a>. Also known as Wôpanâak <a href="https://www.pennpress.org/9780871691859/native-writings-in-massachusett-2-volume-set">or Massachusett</a>, it was one of several Native American languages in the region.</p>

<p>Printing the book would be an important story on its own. But it is even more remarkable because it was <a href="https://eliotbible.web.illinois.edu/the-object/">the first Bible that English colonists published</a> in North America. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.petercmancall.com/">a historian of early America</a>, I believe this Bible sheds important light on relations between New England’s Native peoples and English immigrants, who saw themselves as crucial players in the spread of Protestant Christianity. Consumed with the idea that their culture was superior, many English Protestants <a href="https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300164220/hakluyts-promise/">believed they could conquer North America without much bloodshed</a>: that Indigenous peoples would <a href="https://theconversation.com/beyond-disney-a-1616-portrait-of-pocahontas-shows-how-english-colonizers-saw-indigenous-americans-282221">voluntarily abandon their cultures</a> and embrace the faith of the newcomers.</p>

<p>The historical record is more complex. <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/contested-continent-9780195372786">My 2026 book, “Contested Continent,”</a> details the struggle to control North America in the generations after Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic Ocean. There were many moments, including <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/this-land-is-their-land-9781632869265/">the fabled first Thanksgiving of 1621</a>, when Indigenous peoples and colonists coexisted. But there was <a href="https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/anglo-powhatan-war-second-1622-1632/">brutal violence as well</a>, such as English colonists’ <a href="https://www.laphamsquarterly.org/roundtable/mystic-river-massacre">efforts to destroy the Pequot</a> of southern New England in 1637.</p>

<p>In the aftermath of early warfare, some Puritan clerics looked for new ways to convert Native Americans – and decided religious texts were the answer. </p>

<h2>Puritans and print</h2>

<p>During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther argued that the only infallible source of religious understanding <a href="https://museeprotestant.org/en/notice/luther-and-bible-reading/">was the Bible</a>, a doctrine known as “sola scriptura.” Protestants believed the laity needed to become literate, in order to read Scripture for themselves.</p>

<p>The Puritans embraced this teaching, and in 1638, the Rev. Joseph Glover paid <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/north-americas-first-printing-press/">to transport a printing press to Cambridge</a>, Massachusetts. Two years later, that press published <a href="https://www.americanantiquarian.org/programs-events/perspectives-collection-bay-psalm-book">the Bay Psalm Book</a>, a collection of songs for worship – the first book printed in English North America. </p>

<p>In the years that followed, <a href="https://archive.org/details/catalogueofcolle1892bost/page/152/mode/2up">printers offered many religious tracts</a>, often based on sermons. They believed that print would <a href="https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2039/the-printing-press--the-protestant-reformation/">bring Protestant Christianity to a widening audience</a> and provide guidance for existing believers. </p>

<h2>John Eliot and Cockenoe</h2>

<p>A Puritan minister named John Eliot sailed from England to Boston in 1631 and soon <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674475373">took a leading role</a> in the church at Roxbury, just south of the city. Eliot was so devoted to books that he purportedly brought 23 barrels of them with him from England.</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A painted portrait of a man with long brown hair wearing a black robe and posing with his hand on an open book." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=723&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=723&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=723&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=908&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=908&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771663/original/file-20261112-64-vrg11g.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=908&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">In addition to his missionary work, John Eliot founded Roxbury Latin, a school for boys that is still open today.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_John_Eliot.jpg">Roxbury Latin School/Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>By the 1640s, he began <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Eliot-British-missionary">trying to spread his faith</a> among Native residents of the region. To do so, he needed to be able to communicate with those he hoped to convert, and he understood that books could advance his cause.</p>

<p>Other colonists also hoped that print could foster good relations with the Native residents of New England. The most famous was Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island. “<a href="https://ia803205.us.archive.org/33/items/bub_gb_wOfpAPRxlVYC/bub_gb_wOfpAPRxlVYC.pdf">A Key into the Language of America</a>,” a book he published in London in 1643, <a href="https://historicbostons.org/events/radicals-rebels-and-rejects-1-gdw8b">provided phrases in Narragsansett</a>, another Algonquian language. Such efforts were crucial to Europeans eager to trade with Native peoples – and to those, like Williams, who wanted to <a href="https://www.nps.gov/rowi/learn/historyculture/toknowapeople.htm">spread their culture without violence</a>. </p>

<p>Eliot was intent on translating the Bible. He did not know Wampanoag, but he met an interpreter who impressed him: Cockenoe, <a href="https://biblicalelearning.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Tooker_JohnEliots_First_IndianTeacher.pdf">a Montauk man from Long Island</a> who had been taken captive during the Anglo-Pequot War in 1637. He became crucial to the Cambridge-educated cleric’s cause. </p>

<p>Eliot was unstinting in <a href="https://collections.americanantiquarian.org/EnglishtoAlgonquian/cockenoe">his praise of Cockenoe</a>, whom he called a “pregnant witted young man.” He pronounced words clearly, which was crucial for Eliot: Like almost all Native languages in North America at the time, Wanpanoak did not have a writing system, so Eliot needed to transcribe what he heard.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A faded manuscript page with writing in a Native American language, written using the Roman alphabet." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=791&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=791&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=791&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=994&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=994&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771627/original/file-20261112-64-kct5v9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=994&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">John Eliot’s Bible, which he translated from English to Wampanoag with the interpreter Cockenoe, was published in 1663.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:John_Elliot_Bible,_1663.jpg">Houghton Library, Harvard University via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The ‘Eliot’ Bible</h2>

<p>Cockenoe’s instruction enabled Eliot to produce religious works in Wampanoag, including the Ten Commandments and the Lord’s Prayer. In 1663, printers Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson published “<a href="https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/bibles/interactives/more/other13.html">Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God</a>,” Eliot and Cockenoe’s full translation of the Bible.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/bibles/interactives/more/other13.html">Their Bible</a> included some lines in English so that a literate person could recite the Native words out loud to others, even if they did not know the meaning. Green ordered enough paper to produce 1,000 copies of the book, although it is difficult to know how many existed.</p>

<p>Cockenoe was not the only Indigenous resident who worked on the Bible. <a href="https://bostonathenaeum.org/news/we-have-but-one-man-a-rare-glimpse-into-the-life-and-work-of-james-the-printer/">Wawaus</a>, a Nipmuc man from <a href="https://www.nipmucmuseum.org/history/">what is now central Massachusetts</a>, helped set type for the book. Also known as James Printer, he was studying at <a href="https://peabody.harvard.edu/galleries/digging-veritas-indian-college">Harvard’s Indian College</a>, which had been established in 1655 to spread Christianity among Native peoples. </p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A faded manuscript page from a Bible, with an ornate first letter at the beginning of the text." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=723&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=723&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=723&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=908&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=908&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771631/original/file-20261112-64-qwj459.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=908&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Growing pressure</h2>

<p>Eliot’s efforts to convert Indigenous peoples <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674475373">extended beyond translation</a>, giving him the sobriquet “apostle to the Indians.” </p>

<p>He also worked with <a href="https://collections.americanantiquarian.org/EnglishtoAlgonquian/societyforthepropagation">a missionary society</a> to establish new towns where Algonquian-speaking peoples would abandon their traditional practices and live like colonists. Residents were to halt seasonal migrations, which had been crucial to their economies, and instead live year-round in houses. They were to dress like colonists, follow colonial laws and <a href="https://www.natickhistoricalsociety.org/naticks-beginnings">embrace Protestant religious practices</a>.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, the growth of the colonial population was putting added pressure on Indigenous peoples who lived nearby. By the mid-1670s, any remaining goodwill between many Indigenous peoples and English colonists faded in <a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780809016341/changesinthelandrevisededition/">a contest over limited resources</a>, which was particularly difficult for Native Americans not living in the missionary communities. </p>

<p>In 1675, tensions erupted into what was called <a href="https://historycambridge.org/articles/metacoms-resistance/">Metacom’s or King Philip’s War</a>, named after the Wampanoag leader who led <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/metacoms-war/">a widespread rebellion</a> against colonists. The two-year conflict spread across southern New England and reached the shores of Casco Bay in present-day Maine. According to <a href="https://jlepore.scholars.harvard.edu/">historian Jill Lepore</a>, it was <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/100085/the-name-of-war-by-jill-lepore/">the deadliest war in American history</a>, in proportion to the population.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
