            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Paul Revere’s engraving of Metacom, also called King Philip, who led the Wampanoag during a two-year war with English colonists.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Philip_King_of_Mount_Hope_by_Paul_Revere.jpeg">Yale University Art Gallery/Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Among the victims were the Native converts in the towns Eliot helped to establish, <a href="https://www.natickhistoricalsociety.org/natickhistoricalsociety/king-philips-war">including Natick</a>, a community west of Boston. Colonial authorities rounded them up, transported them to an island in Boston harbor and <a href="https://wwnorton.com/books/New-England-Bound/">sold many into slavery</a>. Even those who escaped the ravages of war found themselves struggling to <a href="https://www.nebraskapress.unl.edu/nebraska-paperback/9780803286191/dispossession-by-degrees/">maintain their shrinking lands</a>.</p>

<h2>A complicated legacy</h2>

<p>Eliot believed that literacy was crucial for spreading his faith. In Cockenoe he found a talented partner. But mastering literacy could be a double-edged sword. </p>

<p>In 1676, in the midst of Metacom’s War, soldiers <a href="https://www.colonialsociety.org/node/1864">came across a note in English</a> in the smoldering ruins of Medfield, a colonial town destroyed by Native Americans. Possibly written by Wawaus, the brief message warned that Indigenous residents <a href="https://stolenrelations.org/wawaus-james-printer/">would fight for years to maintain their lands</a>. </p>

<p>Some colonizers, including Eliot, hoped to avoid using guns and bloodshed to advance their faith. But their goal was still destruction: to eliminate Algonquian cultures. As Wawaus’ note and Algonquian-speaking peoples’ presence in New England today reveal, those efforts failed.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295848/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772037/original/file-20261115-63-t2zybl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=204%2C483%2C5125%2C3416&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Outbreaks caused by falling vaccination rates led to the loss of a public health achievement attained in 2000. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/measles-outbreak-royalty-free-image/2163958662">wildpixel/iStock via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The United States has <a href="https://kffhealthnews.org/public-health/us-measles-elimination-status-lost-outbreaks-continuous-spread-year-paho-cdc/">lost its measles elimination status</a> – an international designation reflecting an absence of <a href="https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WER9243">local measles transmission</a> for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html">since 2000</a>. A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a <a href="https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/2-more-people-die-measles-complications-us-cases-top-5400">formal announcement expected Nov. 17</a>. </p>

<p>Canada lost its measles elimination status <a href="https://theconversation.com/canada-loses-its-official-measles-free-status-and-the-us-will-follow-soon-as-vaccination-rates-fall-269090">in 2025</a>, as did the <a href="https://beaconbio.org/en/report/?reportid=65d8c4f1-e15b-4d3c-8681-f6d10b58c292&amp;utm">United Kingdom and other countries</a> in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.  </p>

<p>These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/causes/index.html">one of the most contagious diseases</a> and still <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-millions-of-people-around-the-world-are-contracting-measles-in-2026-289667">circulates in much of the world</a>. What keeps the disease in check is <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-herd-immunity-a-public-health-expert-and-a-medical-laboratory-scientist-explain-170520">herd immunity</a> – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/global-measles-vaccination/about/index.html">at least 95%</a>. But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine</a>. </p>

<p>I’m an <a href="https://publichealth.uic.edu/profiles/wallace-katrine/">epidemiologist who studies misinformation</a> in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched <a href="https://theconversation.com/vaccine-misinformation-distorts-science-a-biochemist-explains-how-rfk-jr-and-his-lawyers-claims-threaten-public-health-246000">vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage</a> that kept measles from spreading. </p>



<h2>An effective vaccine</h2>

<p>A measles vaccine has <a href="https://theconversation.com/rfk-jr-wants-to-scrutinize-the-vaccine-schedule-but-its-safety-record-is-already-decades-long-271408">existed in the U.S. since 1963</a>. The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/vaccines/index.html">97% effective</a>. A federal program created in 1993 made it <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines-for-children/about/index.html">free for eligible children</a>. After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00053391.htm">dropped more than 99%</a>, and by 2000 measles was <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html">declared eliminated</a>.</p>

<p>But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/377696">maintaining elimination status would require</a> sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dG_ULyeN5d0?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">As multiple measles outbreaks continue across the U.S., international health authorities have announced the loss of its measles elimination status.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html">Before the vaccine</a>, measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the <a href="https://abcnews.com/Health/history-measles-cases-us-meeting-decide-elimination-status/story?id=138042017">official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases</a>. </p>

<p>About <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/signs-symptoms/index.html">1 in 20 children</a> who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called <a href="https://theconversation.com/measles-can-ravage-the-immune-system-and-brain-causing-long-term-damage-a-virologist-explains-252354">immune amnesia</a>, leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.</p>

<p>In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560673/">subacute sclerosing panencephalitis</a>, which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a <a href="https://www.idse.net/Pediatric-Infections/Article/09-25/California-SSPE-Measles-Death/78258">child in Los Angeles died of it</a>.</p>

<h2>A surge of outbreaks – and deaths</h2>

<p>As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">5,412 cases for 2026</a> – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">1 in 6 have been hospitalized</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">Six deaths</a> appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which <a href="https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/cdc-s-new-tracking-method-measles-deaths-puzzles-experts">now relies</a> on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">Pennsylvania</a>, one in <a href="https://www.health.ny.gov/diseases/communicable/measles/data.htm">New York</a> and two in <a href="https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/immunization/measles.htm">Wisconsin</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">Pennsylvania’s outbreak</a> alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">Major outbreaks</a> have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. <a href="https://files.epi.utah.gov/Utah%20measles%20dashboard.html">Utah’s outbreak</a>, which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6041119/us-measles-elimination-status-vaccines-cdc-paho">triggered the loss of elimination status</a>. </p>

<h2>Fertile ground for misinformation</h2>

<p>When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.</p>

<p>Parents who had never seen measles had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/virtualmentor.2012.14.1.fred1-1201">nothing vivid to weigh</a> against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper <a href="https://doi.org/10.4103/0019-5545.82529">fraudulently linking MMR to autism</a> was <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.c696">retracted in 2010</a>, and its author <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/society/2010/may/24/andrew-wakefield-struck-off-gmc">lost his medical license</a>. But the damage was already done, and this myth <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-polling-on-health-information-and-trust/?entry=false-or-unproven-health-claims-belief-in-false-or-unproven-health-claims">persists to this day</a>, even though studies that included <a href="https://www.chop.edu/vaccine-education-center/vaccine-safety/vaccines-and-other-conditions/autism">millions of children have found no link</a>. </p>

<p>During the COVID-19 pandemic, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263746">vaccine misinformation proliferated</a> in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">has fallen every year</a> since the 2019-20 school year.</p>

<p>In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-tracking-poll-on-health-information-and-trust-update-on-common-vaccine-myths/">twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines</a>. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI149072">medical freedom</a> to gain a larger, more <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/31/opinion/anti-vaccine-movement.html">mainstream audience</a>.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Federal policy fuels further confusion</h2>

<p>Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.</p>

<p>On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/delivering-gold-standard-childhood-vaccine-recommendations-for-americans/">MMR to be split into three single-disease shots</a>, which are <a href="https://theconversation.com/executive-order-on-vaccines-bypasses-an-evidence-based-process-that-has-kept-kids-safe-289469">not sold in the United States</a>. There is <a href="https://perma.cc/W2VE-P3YQ">no published evidence</a> that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/21645515.2017.1362515">more chances for missed doses</a>. </p>

<p>Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that <a href="https://theconversation.com/cdc-vs-pennsylvania-why-conflicting-public-health-messages-jeopardize-public-safety-291239">Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths</a> “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While <a href="https://www.factcheck.org/2026/05/a-timeline-of-rfk-jr-s-mixed-messaging-on-the-measles-vaccine/">questioning the vaccine</a> and measles deaths, he has promoted <a href="https://abcnews.com/Health/rfk-jr-claims-measles-treated-vitamin-linked-poor/story?id=119713193">vitamin A and nutrition</a> as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html#cdc_clinical_overview_treat_pat-patient-management">supportive treatment</a>, not a cure or vaccine substitute. </p>

<p>Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26</a>. Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">record 4.2%</a>. </p>

<p>Of this year’s cases, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">96% were unvaccinated or of unknown</a> status. The <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html">92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate</a> leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with <a href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/resources/reports/monitoring-childhood-immunization-at-the-state-level/idaho#coverage">75.2% among Idaho kindergartners</a>, while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html">Adult immunity also has gaps</a>: Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one. </p>

<h2>Roadblocks to recovery</h2>

<p>Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/381556">12 months without continuous transmission</a>. That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.  </p>

<p>But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about.</p>

<p>The Department of Health and Human Services <a href="https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/hearings-rfk-jr-claims-no-responsibility-measles-spread">blames current vaccination gaps</a> on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-cdc-has-a-new-director-now-comes-the-hard-part-289677">CDC Director Erica Schwartz</a> said that the agency would <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/10/health/cdc-measles-elimination-response">not make any changes</a> in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status. </p>

<p>Additionally, <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/delivering-gold-standard-childhood-vaccine-recommendations-for-americans/">orders like August’s</a> about the MMR vaccine, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/federal-judge-temporarily-blocks-rfk-jr-s-vaccine-agenda-an-epidemiologist-answers-questions-parents-may-have-278709">revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations</a>, are <a href="https://www.networkforphl.org/resources/federal-and-state-attacks-on-vaccine-policy/">weakening vaccination efforts</a>. </p>

<p>Also, on top of a <a href="https://ourpublicservice.org/know-the-facts/resource-library/reports/the-cost-of-cutting-american-science-how-federal-cuts-diminish-public-health-capacity">chronically underfunded public health infrastructure </a>, many career public health scientists <a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/03/27/nx-s1-5342414/hhs-doge-rif-rfk-job-cuts">lost their jobs</a> in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-cuts-to-cdc-are-dismantling-its-capacity-to-protect-americans-health-284280">has been substantially weakened</a>.</p>

<p>So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296664/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Lucía Caminos is the first Latina ‘Grand Theft Auto’ lead – these video game characters paved the way</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771650/original/file-20261112-64-navd2h.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=68%2C0%2C2306%2C1537&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">&#39;Grand Theft Auto VI&#39; lead Lucia Caminos is a fiercely ambitious woman who sees crime as a means of escaping the circumstances she&#39;s been born into.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gta6hype.com/_astro/Lucia_Caminos_07.BR2IGyHs_Z1Sq3e2.webp">Rockstar Games</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If the Netflix-exclusive trailer that <a href="https://www.thegamer.com/gta-6-netflix-crashes/">briefly crashed the streaming service</a> in August 2026 is any indication, “<a href="https://www.rockstargames.com/VI">Grand Theft Auto VI</a>” – a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style crime saga set in a satirical, fictionalized Florida – may be <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/after-more-than-a-decade-of-waiting-gta-vi-is-finally-around-the-corner/">the most anticipated video game of all time</a>. </p>

<p>It’s been 13 years since gaming company Rockstar released a new title in its flagship franchise. Fans have spent years <a href="https://www.notebookcheck.net/Vampire-ferris-wheel-GTA-6-fans-dissect-new-clip-over-one-odd-detail.1325182.0.html">dissecting leaked footage</a>, constructing elaborate theories about the game’s mechanics and even attempting <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DAEuEjirHJc&amp;t=530s">to reconstruct its fictional map using real-world geography</a>.</p>

<p>But as a Latino studies scholar <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/teaching-games-and-game-studies-in-the-literature-classroom-9781350269750/">who teaches</a> and <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/1/article/957948">researches video games</a>, I’m most excited by the fact that “Grand Theft Auto VI” is the first title in the series to feature a Latina lead character: <a href="https://gta.fandom.com/es/wiki/Luc%C3%ADa_Caminos">Lucía Caminos</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://elpais.com/tecnologia/2026-10-16/de-lara-croft-a-lucia-caminos-por-que-todavia-molesta-que-una-mujer-sea-protagonista-de-un-videojuego.html">Not everyone is thrilled</a> about a female protagonist – sexism, after all, <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctt2005rgq">remains a persistent issue</a> in the gaming community.</p>

<p>But it nonetheless represents a watershed moment, as Latina video game characters have historically played second fiddle. Latino popular culture scholar <a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/9781137361783">Frederick Luis Aldama</a> has pointed out how Latinos usually exist as obstacles for players to overcome rather than heroes whose stories players get to experience firsthand. </p>

<p>At the same time, a host of Latina characters throughout video game history – some playable, most not – paved the way for Lucía. Together, they show how representation is less about skin color and more about connection, complexity and character development.</p>

<h2>A ‘badass Latina’ who travels the world</h2>

<p>In 1985, Carmen Sandiego was introduced as a criminal mastermind in “<a href="https://computerhistory.org/blog/where-in-the-world-is-carmen-sandiego/">Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego?</a>” </p>

<p>Players must pursue Carmen as she leaves a trail of clues across the globe. But Brøderbund, the game’s developer, left Carmen’s ethnic identity and origins ambiguous. </p>

<p>While researching the <a href="https://archives.museumofplay.org/repositories/3/resources/37">Brøderbund Collection</a> at the Strong Museum of Play, I learned that the game’s creators <a href="https://www.museumofplay.org/blog/driven-by-play-a-reflection-on-carmen-sandiego-freedom-and-games-between-1980-and-2000/">originally imagined Carmen as a man named Estaban Devious</a> who was born in Andorra, a tiny country in the Pyrenees with a large Spanish-speaking population. Brøderbund eventually settled on Carmen Sandiego – a name deemed exotic and befitting of a world traveler. </p>

<p>Despite Carmen’s unclear origins, Latinas have long connected with her. Actress <a href="https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1752221/">Gina Rodriguez</a> was so taken with Carmen as a kid that she jumped at the chance to voice Carmen in the animated series “<a href="https://www.netflix.com/title/80167821">Carmen Sandiego</a>,” which premiered on Netflix in 2019 and ran for four seasons. <a href="https://www.brit.co/gina-rodriguez-carmen-sandiego-netflix-interview/">According to Rodriguez</a>, Carmen was “an incredible, strong, feminist, badass Latina who was going around the world. … I wanted to be just like her.” This cartoon gave Carmen a clear backstory – she was Argentine – and complicated her portrayal as a villain by having her turn on the very criminal organization she once belonged to.</p>

<p>With the show introducing Carmen Sandiego to a new generation of kids, <a href="https://carmensandiego-game.com/">new titles continue to appear</a>. To coincide with Carmen’s 40th anniversary, “<a href="https://carmensandiego-game.com/">Carmen Sandiego</a>” was released in 2025. It finally makes Carmen a playable character.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">

            </figcaption>

<h2>A change of heart</h2>

<p>Like Carmen Sandiego, Isabela Keyes is a villain. One of the antagonists of the 2006 game “<a href="https://www.deadrising.com/en/">Dead Rising</a>,” Isabela is the sister of Carlito Keyes, who initiates a zombie outbreak in Colorado.</p>

<p>Players discover that Isabela and Carlito infected people with the zombie virus to avenge the destruction of their hometown, Santa Cabeza, a fictional Central American village. The U.S. government had been experimenting with the virus there and destroyed the town to cover up its research.</p>

          </figure>

<p>But Isabela eventually realizes that she and Carlito have gone too far. She has a change of heart and ends up turning against her brother. </p>

<p>I think of Isabela as an important Latina video game character because she’s not simply included as a pretty face. That’s too often been the case for Latina characters, whether it’s Cynthia Velasquez in “Silent Hill 4” – whose alternate costume in the game <a href="https://silenthill.fandom.com/wiki/Cynthia_Velasquez?file=Cynthia_2.png">made her look like a Playboy bunny</a> – or <a href="https://tekken.fandom.com/wiki/Katarina_Alves">Katarina Alves</a> in “Tekken 7,” whose default and alternate costumes prominently feature her thong.</p>

<p>Capcom, the studio that produced the game, nonetheless marketed Isabela as a sex symbol. The question of how to interpret this sort of sexualization has divided gamers and scholars. On the one hand, many game designers still see their target audience as heterosexual men. However, <a href="https://www.upress.umn.edu/9781452954998/ready-player-two/">women now make up half the gaming market</a>, and overtly sexualized characters, which continue to appear, could further <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/01634437231219383">the sexism that bedevils the industry</a>.</p>

<h2>Secret love</h2>

<p>Video games have historically featured <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/jj.24215709.13?seq=1">few queer characters</a>, <a href="https://www.publicbooks.org/queer-representation-videogames/">let alone queer Latino characters</a>.</p>

<p>But indie games, which are developed outside major studios and often prioritize creative experimentation over commercial conventions, have generally been more welcoming to LGBTQ+ narratives and representation.</p>

<p>Fullbright’s 2013 exploration game “<a href="https://www.ign.com/articles/2013/08/15/gone-home-review">Gone Home</a>” tells a 1990s coming-out story. Players explore the empty Oregon home of Katie Greenbriar and gradually learn the story of her younger sister, Sam, and Sam’s Mexican American girlfriend, Lonnie DeSoto, who hopes to one day join the military.</p>

<p>Though Lonnie is not a playable character, players piece together her experiences through letters and other clues. They learn about the challenges Lonnie faces as a Latina lesbian in the Junior Reserve Officers Training Corps, a high school program that teaches military-style leadership and discipline. By incorporating aspects of 1990s zine culture, the U.S. military’s <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7249/mg1056osd.10">Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell policy</a> toward homosexuality and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10304312.2019.1567685">the feminist punk movement Riot Grrrl</a>, “Gone Home” accurately and realistically captured the hopes and fears of being LGBTQ+ in the 1990s.</p>

<h2>Getting a chance to play Latina</h2>

<p>For years, playable Latina characters were pretty much nonexistent. Opportunities almost exclusively came from the large rosters of fighting games – characters like <a href="https://snk.fandom.com/wiki/%C3%81ngel">Ángel</a> in the 2001 game “King of Fighters” and <a href="https://tekken.fandom.com/wiki/Christie_Monteiro">Christie Monteiro</a> in “Tekken,” also released in 2001.</p>

<p>Over the past decade, that’s started to change. </p>

<p><a href="https://overwatch.fandom.com/wiki/Sombra">Sombra is a Mexican hacker</a> and one of the most prominent characters in the 2016 futuristic shooter “Overwatch.” Born Olivia Colomar, she was orphaned as a child and grew up in Mexico, where she developed extraordinary computer skills. She works with the game’s antagonists but pursues her own agenda of unraveling a global conspiracy.</p>

<p><a href="https://valorant.fandom.com/wiki/Reyna">Zyanya Mondragón</a>, better known as Reyna, is a Mexican character in the 2020 futuristic shooter “VALORANT.” Reyna is a supernatural warrior who absorbs the life energy of enemies she kills, using it to heal herself and grow stronger. But her bloodthirsty nature has a deeply personal motivation: She needs the life energy she harvests to keep her younger sister, Lucia, alive. </p>

<p>These two characters have compelling pasts and aren’t clear-cut antagonists. However, they still sometimes fall victim to the “<a href="https://utpress.utexas.edu/9780292714939/">sexy Latina</a>” stereotype. For example, in a segment of Conan O'Brien’s Clueless Gamer series, in which the blundering comedian tries out new video games, O'Brien <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X8bjvoHOSFs">repeatedly ogles over Sombra’s body</a>.</p>

<p>Lucía Caminos will join just a handful of playable Latina characters, like <a href="https://gearsofwar.fandom.com/wiki/Kait_Diaz">Kait Diaz</a> from “Gears of War,” in what are known as “<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AAA_(video_game_industry)">AAA games</a>” – titles with the biggest marketing and development budgets. But unlike the “Gears of War” franchise, which was Xbox-only on release, “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be released simultaneously on PlayStation 5, Xbox and the PC.</p>

<p>Yes, Lucía Caminos is an attractive young woman who breaks the law. But richly developed video game characters can move beyond stereotypes and give players new ways to imagine marginalized people as heroes. Rather than judging characters like Lucía as examples of either good or bad representation, it might be better to think about how players can reinterpret their stories, see them as role models and identify with their struggles. </p>

<p>After all, gamers have been doing just that since Carmen Sandiego.</p>

It’s been 13 years since gaming company Rockstar released a new title in its flagship franchise
Fans have spent years dissecting leaked footage , constructing elaborate theories about the game’s mechanics and even attempting to reconstruct its fictional map using real-world geography

<title>Rumi is one of America’s most popular poets – but translations often strip his poetry of its Islamic roots</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771121/original/file-20261110-78-9d77b.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5760%2C3840&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Whirling dervishes, part of a Sufi order formed soon after the death of Rumi, perform the devotional prayer at a mosque in Konya, Turkey.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/konya-mevlana-mosque-and-whirling-dervish-show-royalty-free-image/1042924280?phrase=rumi%20sketch&amp;adppopup=true">Atilla Alp Bolukbasi/iStock via Getty Images plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Every December, thousands of visitors gather in Konya, Turkey, to mark the death of the 13th-century poet Jalal al-Din Rumi. His followers call the night “<a href="https://www.kosu.org/world-news/world-news/2021-12-25/photos-whirling-dervish-ritual-honors-rumi-the-sufi-mystic-poet">Shab-e ‘Arūs</a>,” the wedding night, and it is the moment they believe he was united with God.</p>

<p>Following Rumi’s death in 1273, his disciples formed the <a href="https://mevlana.net/mevlevi_order.html">Mevlevi order</a>, a Sufi brotherhood whose members are known in the West as the “whirling dervishes.” A dervish, from a Persian word for a poor person, is a member of a Sufi order who has committed to a life of spiritual discipline under a teacher. The Mevlevi order spread, and its lodges became centers of music and poetry. Mevlevi musicians <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9781474491884">helped shape Ottoman classical music</a>, and the whirling dervish remains one of Turkey’s most recognizable cultural symbols today.</p>

<p>On the anniversary of Rumi’s death, white-robed dervishes perform a ceremony known as <a href="https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/mevlevi-sema-ceremony-00100">Sema</a>. The ceremony <a href="https://yakegm.ktb.gov.tr/TR-345100/mevlevi-sema-ceremony.html">opens with a hymn praising the Prophet Muhammad</a>, followed by the sound of the “ney,” or reed flute. Accompanied by drums and chanted poetry, the dervishes then turn slowly around the hall, right palm raised to receive God’s blessing and left palm lowered to pass it on to others. For the Mevlevis, the whirling is not a performance but a form of worship, a remembrance of God carried out with the whole body.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A Sufi mystic wearing a turban and a blue tunic reads a book while seated on the floor." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=670&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=670&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=670&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=842&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=842&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771117/original/file-20261110-78-9sotmd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=842&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">A sketch of the poet Rumi.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%D9%85%D9%88%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%A7_%D8%A7%D8%AB%D8%B1_%D8%AD%D8%B3%DB%8C%D9%86_%D8%A8%D9%87%D8%B2%D8%A7%D8%AF_(cropped).jpg">Hossein Behzad via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the United States, thousands of miles away, the same poet’s words appear on wedding programs, yoga studio walls and social media feeds. Rumi is <a href="https://www.csmonitor.com/1997/1125/112597.us.us.3.html">one of the best-selling poets</a> in the U.S. Despite this, many Americans may not know how deeply the Muslim legal scholar and preacher’s poetry is steeped in religion.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://harvard.academia.edu/PeterDziedzic">a scholar of Sufism</a>, the mystical tradition within Islam, I see a gap between these two Rumis – the Muslim mystic revered in Konya and the spiritual sage quoted on Instagram. The popular English translations that made Rumi famous strip the spiritual depth of his writing, which comes from his Islamic faith.</p>

<h2>Who was Rumi?</h2>

<p>Rumi was <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Rumi">born in 1207</a> in Balkh, in present-day Afghanistan. As armies of the Mongol empire – the largest contiguous land empire in history, which at its height stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe – advanced across Central Asia, his family moved west, eventually settling in Konya. </p>

<p>Like his father, the preacher Baha al-Din Walad, Rumi trained in Islamic law and theology and became a respected teacher. His life changed in 1244, when he met Shams of Tabriz, a wandering Sufi teacher. Their <a href="https://www.themuseumoftime.com/post/shams-tabrizi-rumi-relationship">intense companionship</a> upended Rumi’s scholarly life.</p>

<p>After Shams disappeared a few years later, Rumi poured his longing into thousands of lyric poems, later gathered as the <a href="https://www.rumionfire.com/shams/">Divan-e Shams</a>. Most of these are ghazals: short love poems built on a single repeating rhyme, many of them composed during gatherings of music and dance. </p>

<p>Rumi’s masterpiece came later and took a different form – the “masnavi.”</p>

<h2>What is a 'masnavi’?</h2>

<p>A “masnavi” is a type of <a href="https://www.writersdigest.com/write-better-poetry/masnavi-or-mathnawi-poetic-forms">Persian poetic form</a> built from rhyming couplets.</p>

<p>The two lines of each couplet rhyme with each other, and the next couplet can switch to a new rhyme. Because the poet never has to sustain a single rhyme across the whole poem, the form can run on almost indefinitely, which made it a favored vehicle for long poems. <a href="https://worldliteraturetoday.org/blog/cultural-cross-sections/attar-sufi-poet-and-master-rumi-sholeh-wolpe">Other Sufi poets</a> used it to compose spiritual epics.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Rumi’s own “Masnavi-ye Ma'navi,” or “Spiritual Couplets,” better known as “the Masnavi,” is one of the genre’s most celebrated examples. At the urging of his disciple Husam al-Din Chelebi, Rumi began dictating it around 1258 and continued until his death, producing some <a href="https://dar-al-masnavi.org/about_masnavi.html">25,000 couplets</a> across six books.</p>

<p>Rumi’s “Masnavi” opens with the <a href="https://www.dar-al-masnavi.org/n-I-0001.html">song of a reed flute</a> lamenting its separation from the reed bed, an enduring Sufi metaphor of the soul longing to return to its divine source. What follows is less a single story than a vast, winding conversation that includes animal fables, bawdy tales, Quranic stories and reflections on the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad and those who came before him.</p>

<p>Rumi held his “Masnavi” in high regard. In the Arabic preface to its first book, he described it as “<a href="https://dar-al-masnavi.org/about_masnavi.html">the roots of the roots of the roots of religion</a>” and “the explainer of the Quran.” That is a bold claim, but it reflects how the poem works. Its couplets are threaded with Quranic verses, often quoted in the original Arabic, which Rumi then unfolds through stories and images to draw out their deeper meanings. </p>

<p>Later admirers went further. A famous Persian verse calls Rumi’s Masnavi “<a href="https://bridgingcultures-muslimjourneys.org/items/show/191">the Quran in the Persian tongue</a>,” a line <a href="https://fis-iran.org/our-programs/noruz-lectures/rumi-icon-man/">traditionally attributed</a> to the 15th-century poet Jami. For centuries, Muslims from the Balkans to South Asia have gathered in circles to <a href="https://jrp.scu.ac.ir/article_14795.html?lang=en">read and study the “Masnavi”</a> line by line. </p>

<h2>Lost in translation</h2>

<p>Translating any poem involves trade-offs – between sound and sense, between keeping the original’s rhyme and meter and capturing its meaning, and between staying close to the text and making it feel natural to a new audience. With Rumi, the stakes are especially high because so much of his meaning lives in the religious world his poems draw on. Faithful translations exist, but they are not the ones most Americans read. </p>

<p>Scholars such as <a href="https://explore.trin.cam.ac.uk/assets/nicholson/">Reynold Nicholson</a> produced careful English translations of Rumi in the early 20th century, but the versions most Americans know are something different. </p>

<p>The most popular are by the American poet <a href="https://www.english.uga.edu/directory/people/coleman-barks">Coleman Barks</a>, whose books popularized Rumi from the 1970s onward. Barks <a href="https://www.reviewofreligions.org/47939/a-muslim-cleric-from-iran-is-one-of-americas-bestselling-poets-jalaluddin-rumi/">did not read Persian</a>. Instead, he reworked earlier scholarly translations into free-verse American English, a process Duke University scholar <a href="https://islamicstudies.duke.edu/profile/omid-safi/">Omid Safi</a> <a href="https://berkeleydivinity.yale.edu/posts/2025-11-17-72-rumi-love-and-mysticism-with-omid-safi">calls</a> “a double translation.”</p>

<p><a href="https://religion.rutgers.edu/people/core-faculty/people/303-graduate/889-mojaddedi-jawid">Jawid Mojaddedi</a>, who translated the “Masnavi” starting in 2004, <a href="https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/the-erasure-of-islam-from-the-poetry-of-rumi">told The New Yorker</a>: “The Rumi that people love is very beautiful in English, and the price you pay is to cut the culture and religion.” </p>

<p>References to the Quran, the Prophet and Muslim ritual are often softened or dropped. Where Rumi writes “God,” Barks sometimes substitutes “the Beloved.”</p>

<p>Take one of Barks’ best-loved lines – “There are hundreds of ways to kneel and kiss the ground.” As Safi points out, Rumi’s Persian refers to “ruku” and “sujud,” the bowing and prostration of the Muslim ritual prayer performed five times a day. The English is lovely, but it turns a specific Muslim act of worship into a general image of reverence.</p>

<p>Or consider one of Rumi’s most quoted lines in English – “Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field. I’ll meet you there.” A closer rendering of the Persian reads: “Beyond Islam and unbelief, there is a desert plain.” </p>

            </figcaption>

<p>In other words, Rumi is not dismissing faith or morality. He is making a classic Sufi claim that the deepest love of God lies beyond the labels people use to sort believers from unbelievers. That is a striking thing for a Muslim jurist and preacher to say, and it carries its full force only when the reader knows who is saying it. The popular version turns it into generic advice about not judging others.</p>

<p>These are not isolated choices. Across the popular versions, the world Rumi lived in — the Quran he quoted, the prayers he performed, the prophets whose stories he retold — is largely absent.</p>

<h2>Why should we care?</h2>

<p>It might be tempting to treat all this as a debate for specialists, but for millions of Americans, Rumi is one of the few Muslim voices they have ever read. How he is translated shapes how they understand not only the poet, but the tradition he came from.</p>

<p>Safi has described the erasure of Islam from these New Age versions as “<a href="https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/the-erasure-of-islam-from-the-poetry-of-rumi">spiritual colonialism</a>,” a process of bypassing and erasing a spiritual landscape that has been lived and breathed by Muslims across the world. Western readers embrace the beauty of Rumi’s poetry while setting aside the faith that produced it and the communities that have treasured it for centuries.</p>

<p>None of this means Americans should stop reading Rumi in English. Barks and others have introduced millions of people to a poet they might never have encountered. Additionally, newer verse translations of the “Masnavi,” such as <a href="https://bosphorusreview.com/review-the-masnavi-trs-by-mojaddedi">Mojaddedi’s six-volume edition</a>, try to carry over both its form and its Islamic framework.</p>

<p>The larger task is to read Rumi as Muslims from Turkey and Iran to Afghanistan and South Asia have read him for centuries – as a poet whose expansive vision grew out of his faith, not in spite of it.</p>

<p>At a time when Muslims are often cast as outsiders in American public life, presenting one of the world’s most beloved poets as spiritual in spite of Islam, rather than because of it, reinforces a damaging story.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289346/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Annual water-quality reports don’t tell the full story of what you’re drinking</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770363/original/file-20261105-64-lwwx78.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C4000&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">What&#39;s in tap water isn&#39;t always visible, but different compounds can make you healthier or sicker.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/pouring-a-glass-of-water-from-a-kitchen-faucet-in-santa-ana-news-photo/2150231449">Leonard Ortiz/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Water is vital to life, which is part of why we study what’s in it. </p>

<p>Drinking water isn’t just H₂O – though there are over 15 septillion molecules of it in a standard glass. It also contains natural minerals, dissolved organic and biological matter, and substances that enter from agriculture, industry, consumer products and water treatment. </p>

<p>Most of these substances are harmless at the concentrations typically found in water. Some are <a href="https://doi.org/10.11138/ccmbm/2016.13.3.173">beneficial, and even essential</a>, such as sodium, fluoride and calcium ions, which build strong bones and teeth. Additionally, these ions balance electrolytes that regulate bodily function. </p>

<p>In fact, drinking large quantities of completely demineralized or distilled water can disrupt the body’s electrolyte balance. This water would dilute the natural sodium levels in blood, <a href="https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/hyponatremia-low-sodium-level-blood">potentially causing hyponatremia</a>, a condition with symptoms such as nausea, headache, confusion and seizures.</p>

<p>Most people encounter water-quality science through an <a href="https://www.epa.gov/ccr/understanding-your-annual-water-quality-report">annual report from their local water company</a>. It’s usually a couple of pages long with chemical names and numbers in a table. It lists various compounds that may exist in the water, summarizes what has been found in tests of the water source, and explains whether the water meets <a href="https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/national-primary-drinking-water-regulations">government-set standards that promote and protect public health and safety</a>.</p>

<p>These reports provide important information about drinking water safety, but they are not a complete inventory of every substance scientists can detect or are working to understand.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=lLTWb2IAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">We</a>
<a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ojchfXkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">study</a> a range of contaminants, chemical and biological, that are found in drinking water, with the goal of developing technologies to further safeguard public health. This includes pollutants and pathogens that are not included on an annual water report.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man stands in a garage next to large canisters of drinking water." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770438/original/file-20261106-64-qnhqz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<h2>A secret world of sneaky water pollutants</h2>

<p>Consider perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, more commonly known as <a href="https://www.epa.gov/pfas/our-current-understanding-human-health-and-environmental-risks-pfas">PFAS</a> and also called “forever chemicals” because they persist in the environment for a long time. These are a large family of chemicals used in consumer products because they resist water, oil and heat.</p>

<p>Research has linked exposure to certain PFAS with <a href="https://www.ewg.org/news-insights/news/2024/03/pfas-and-developmental-and-reproductive-toxicity-ewg-fact-sheet">adverse chronic health effects</a>, such as endocrine disruption, low birth weight in fetuses and certain types of cancer.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/and-polyfluoroalkyl-substances-pfas">Federal drinking water standards</a> now limit the amount of two common types of PFAS found in the environment to 4 parts per trillion, a level extremely hard to detect even on advanced analytical equipment. However, the broader chemical family includes many others whose occurrence and health effects are less understood by scientists and completely missed by the public or policy.</p>

<p>The challenge that water-quality engineers face is not simply to determine whether PFAS, or other compounds and pollutants, are present. Rather, researchers need to understand the concentrations of those chemicals in the water, how people are exposed to them, what their effects on the body are, and how effectively different treatment technologies can remove or destroy them.</p>

<h2>What doesn’t kill you … might later</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/pharmaceuticals-water">Pharmaceutical residues</a> from medicine that passes through people’s bodies enter sewage systems. Agricultural chemicals such as pesticides flow off croplands into waterways. Both of these types of waste can break down into new, <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/news/pesticides-and-their-degradation-products-common-groundwater-low-concentrations-unlikely-be">less studied compounds</a> as they move through soil and water, eventually collecting in groundwater or wastewater to be treated and redistributed. The potential long-term effects of these lesser-studied compounds are not fully understood. </p>

<p>Water treatment plants often use chlorine as part of the disinfection process. But when chlorine reacts with natural organic matter, such as decayed plants and microorganisms, it forms <a href="https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/environment/water/factsheet/ddbp.html">disinfection byproducts</a>. These byproducts include chemicals such as trihalomethanes, which are known carcinogens that must be removed with further treatment before the water is safe to drink.</p>

<p>Some contaminants pose an immediate threat; others pose threats that accumulate over time. For instance, ingesting <a href="https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241516198">microplastics in drinking water</a> may not hurt you right now, but they are being <a href="https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20220512-the-chemicals-that-linger-for-decades-in-your-blood">detected in people’s blood</a> years after exposure. We water-quality scientists want to know not only what’s in the water, but what it might do to your body right away or across decades.</p>

<h2>Bad to drink, even worse to breathe</h2>

<p>The timescale and route of exposure of waterborne contaminants matter, too. If stagnant pipes are left unused for a long time, bacteria can build up. Then, when people start a shower or an outdoor fountain, that bacteria travels into the air in mist. This poses a different kind of threat than exposure to a chemical pollutant in drinking water because this would lead to bacteria infection. </p>

<p>For example, when there is a large buildup of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/legionella/causes/index.html"><em>Legionella spp.</em> </a>, a group of bacteria that can grow in drinking water distribution systems and power plant cooling towers when condensation pools, people who inhale the water vapor can develop Legionnaires’ disease, an acute form of pneumonia. Waterborne pathogens and their associated infections account for billions of dollars in maintenance and healthcare costs annually. </p>

<h2>Hazards, risk and Flint as an example</h2>

<p>Moreover, it is important to distinguish what is hazardous and how it could eventually become a human health risk. In the case of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/casper/php/publications-links/flint-water-crisis.html">Flint, Michigan</a>, lead in a water pipe is a hazard, but as long as the water flowing through it is <a href="https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/basic-information-about-lead-drinking-water">chemically stable and doesn’t react with lead from the pipes</a>, the immediate risk to human health is low.</p>

<p>In the city’s 2014 water crisis, water from a new source was not chemically treated to reduce its ability to pick up lead from the pipes. By 2016, people had been ordered not to drink the water anymore because it was contaminated with dangerous levels of lead, which can <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/lead-poisoning/symptoms-causes/syc-20354717">cause neurological problems and impair brain function</a>.</p>

<p>The real questions go beyond just looking at what’s in water, to include what kinds of dangers are there, whether immediate like Legionnaires’ disease or chronic like lead poisoning or cancer. Regulatory standards don’t always address every potential source or type of contamination. </p>

<p>The next time you review your local water report, don’t just look at what is being monitored; consider what may not be on the list at all.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294766/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: What's in tap water isn't always visible, but different compounds can make you healthier or sicker
Leonard Ortiz/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images Water is vital to life, which is part of why we study what’s in it
Drinking water isn’t just H₂O – though there are over 15 septillion molecules of it in a standard glass
It also contains natural minerals, dissolved organic and biological matter, and substances that enter from agriculture, industry, consumer products and water treatment
Most of these substances are harmless at the concentrations typically found in water
Some are beneficial, and even essential , such as sodium, fluoride and calcium ions, which build strong bones and teeth
Additionally, these ions balance electrolytes that regulate bodily function
In fact, drinking large quantities of completely demineralized or distilled water can disrupt the body’s electrolyte balance
This water would dilute the natural sodium levels in blood, potentially causing hyponatremia , a condition with symptoms such as nausea, headache, confusion and seizures
Most people encounter water-quality science through an annual report from their local water company
It’s usually a couple of pages long with chemical names and numbers in a table

It lists various compounds that may exist in the water, summarizes what has been found in tests of the water source, and explains whether the water meets government-set standards that promote and protect public health and safety
These reports provide important information about drinking water safety, but they are not a complete inventory of every substance scientists can detect or are working to understand
We study a range of contaminants, chemical and biological, that are found in drinking water, with the goal of developing technologies to further safeguard public health
This includes pollutants and pathogens that are not included on an annual water report
In some communities, high levels of contaminants have led water utilities to supply bottled water to customers

Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images A secret world of sneaky water pollutants Consider perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, more commonly known as PFAS and also called “forever chemicals” because they persist in the environment for a long time
These are a large family of chemicals used in consumer products because they resist water, oil and heat
Research has linked exposure to certain PFAS with adverse chronic health effects , such as endocrine disruption, low birth weight in fetuses and certain types of cancer

Federal drinking water standards now limit the amount of two common types of PFAS found in the environment to 4 parts per trillion, a level extremely hard to detect even on advanced analytical equipment
However, the broader chemical family includes many others whose occurrence and health effects are less understood by scientists and completely missed by the public or policy
The challenge that water-quality engineers face is not simply to determine whether PFAS, or other compounds and pollutants, are present

Rather, researchers need to understand the concentrations of those chemicals in the water, how people are exposed to them, what their effects on the body are, and how effectively different treatment technologies can remove or destroy them
What doesn’t kill you … might later Pharmaceutical residues from medicine that passes through people’s bodies enter sewage systems
Agricultural chemicals such as pesticides flow off croplands into waterways
Both of these types of waste can break down into new, less studied compounds as they move through soil and water, eventually collecting in groundwater or wastewater to be treated and redistributed
The potential long-term effects of these lesser-studied compounds are not fully understood
Water treatment plants often use chlorine as part of the disinfection process
But when chlorine reacts with natural organic matter, such as decayed plants and microorganisms, it forms disinfection byproducts
These byproducts include chemicals such as trihalomethanes, which are known carcinogens that must be removed with further treatment before the water is safe to drink
Some contaminants pose an immediate threat; others pose threats that accumulate over time
For instance, ingesting microplastics in drinking water may not hurt you right now, but they are being detected in people’s blood years after exposure
