title: Trump closes an AI loophole
excerpt: President Donald Trump departs the White House on November 16, 2026, ahead of a trip to China and the Philippines. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This st
body: President Donald Trump departs the White House on November 16, 2026, ahead of a trip to China and the Philippines. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is closing a global AI chip loophole that the Jensen Huang scandal put in the spotlight
What’s changing? The Commerce Department is trying to make it harder for China to access top-of-the-line AI microchips like those made by Nvidia
Currently, China is able to dodge export rules by renting computing power from third-country data centers, which can legally buy American-made chips that China can’t

But under the rule issued Monday, which is set to take effect in 90 days, data centers in a handful of countries will face new export restrictions on chips — including a requirement that they perform “robust due diligence on their customers” to make sure that they aren’t evading an export ban.  What’s the context? Huang, who resigned from Nvidia last week, was brought down in part by his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an alleged Chinese spy ( kind of ) and an executive at a Singapore-based tech company, Megaspeed, that was renting compute to Chinese firms — exactly the kind of thing that the new rule aims to crack down on.  What’s the big picture? The Nvidia scandal is front and center
But under the hood, there’s also some Trump administration infighting going on
As a statement announcing the new rule notes, it was written not by the Commerce Department, which is issuing it, but by the Treasury Department and the National Security Council

That’s conspicuous because Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has done his best to throw Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under the bus for the scandal, saying that Lutnick’s department failed to restrict Megaspeed’s access to advanced AI chips sooner

Where’s President Donald Trump in all this? As of Monday, off to China and the Philippines for a multiday trip that will feature a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.  For now, though, Trump is standing by Lutnick — and even by Jensen Huang, saying Monday that he “would certainly not mind” seeing him return as Nvidia CEO (the Nvidia board has already shut down the possibility)

And with that, it’s time to log off… One of my colleagues described this story about Anny Aviram, a now-retired conservator at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, as “a true balm for the weary soul,” and it lives up to the billing
As always, thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: How to actually fix America’s air traffic control system
excerpt: What happened on Friday was only the latest symptom of an aging air traffic control system. | Adam Gray/Getty Images On Friday evening, in the midst of the seco
body: What happened on Friday was only the latest symptom of an aging air traffic control system. | Adam Gray/Getty Images On Friday evening, in the midst of the second-longest closure ever of US airspace, I bought two plane tickets and found myself contemplating, possibly for the first time, the list of hidden fees tacked onto my fare.  I had forked over $16.95 for a US transportation tax, plus $5.30 for a flight segment tax, both of which pool into the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, which will ultimately contribute to the Federal Aviation Administration’s work, thereby ensuring that my flight from New York to Florida lands smoothly
But though one might expect my $22.25 — enough to pay an air traffic trainee’s salary for about an hour — would go directly into the FAA’s coffers, it does not

In fact, the FAA needs to get congressional approval every time it taps into its trust fund, a political bottleneck that has for decades kept the FAA from making the critical long-term modernization projects it needs to make sure that a single botched cable job is not enough to bring down the busiest airspace in the world
In the days since all air travel shut down across the United States, we’ve learned a great deal about what happened and why

But the best response to the crisis — and the path to preventing it from happening again (and again and again) — may well be found in shortening the path that my $22.25 takes on its way to the beleaguered agency that needs it so badly

It’s a solution that transformed air travel in Canada — which turned its air traffic control system around three decades ago — and it might yet help guarantee on-time departures here in the United States, too

View Link In the aftermath of the groundstop on Friday, college football teams delayed their kickoff times and Microsoft — whose Outlook outage suddenly became only the second-most disruptive telecommunications issue last week — issued an inadvertently cheeky disclaimer saying “it wasn’t us.” The band Hoobastank performed an impromptu rendition of their 2004 hit “The Reason” aboard a Southwest Airlines flight, before the actual reason for the delay was even clear

But while rumors have swirled over whether the disruption could be the work of a rogue AI cyberattack , the real reason why the FAA closed America’s airspace for only the third time since 9/11 now appears to have been embarrassingly mundane. “They were putting in new equipment and new technology,” said Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, in a press briefing on Friday, “and that new equipment was overwhelming the older system.”  There is, to be sure, plenty of new equipment to be put in, and not just at the tiny, two-runway airport in El Dorado, Arkansas, where the trouble began

The physical bones of our air traffic control system were installed back when many of Hoobastank’s Gen X fans were still in diapers, and the bulk of this vital system — which tells pilots when and where it’s safe to land — has not been upgraded since the 1980s
Most control towers still track airplanes using thin strips of cardstock , while 3.5-inch floppy disks remain the medium of choice for uploading weather forecasts
And copper wires, instead of more modern fiber optic cables, still transmit large swaths of data between air traffic control facilities
In 2024, the Government Accountability Office found indications that 76 percent of the FAA’s systems were or could be unsustainable because of factors like aging equipment
Just a few months ago, a single severed cable grounded flights at some of the nation’s busiest airports
And for years, air traffic controllers have been sounding the alarm about chronic understaffing, unsustainable workloads, and an accumulation of safety complaints

What happened on Friday was only the latest symptom of an aging air traffic control system, one that has suffered from deferred maintenance for so long that even trying to fix things can make the whole network go haywire

The Trump administration, to its credit, has made upgrading this decades-old system a priority of its transportation agenda, spurred in part by a tragedy over the Potomac last year in which an Army helicopter collided with a commercial airliner , killing 67 people.  But making sure that this fiasco doesn’t happen again will require more than just plying the FAA with another $50 billion in cash , per Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s pleas to Congress

It might require doing away entirely with the political wrangling that keeps the FAA thirsting for your airline fees, and giving it easier access to those hidden fees tacked on to your boarding pass and mine. “Modernization in the US is a political battle,” John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University, told me

But in other countries like Canada, air traffic control “modernization is very much a functional battle,” made possible by predictable “funding it can use to modernize at its own pace, rather than fighting constant battles for congressional appropriations.”  Even $50 billion may not be enough to fix what’s wrong with the FAA, not least of all because a single lump sum — no matter how gigantic — won’t address the funding bottleneck that makes it hard to keep things running day in and day out. “They’re throwing a number at it, and there’s no detail behind the number,” he said. “What’s the architecture of the solution?” In fact, there is a better way to fix our airspace, and our neighbors to the north might be able to chart the course

How Canada fixed its air traffic control system In the 1990s, Canada’s air traffic control system was bogged down by many of the same problems that the American system still suffers from now.  Audits at the time found that chronic staffing shortages and unreasonable expectations of overtime were playing a serious role in air traffic incidents such as dangerously close calls between passenger jets

Meanwhile, Canada’s transportation department, Transport Canada, had gone seriously over budget and behind schedule while trying to modernize the country’s radar system, par for the course of a system under strain
At the time, as in the US, a fee tacked onto flights went into a fund under the control of the Canadian government, meaning that Transport Canada often found itself begging Parliament for more cash
But this changed in 1996, after a broad coalition of fed-up pilots, airlines, and air traffic controllers rallied behind a new governance structure for Canada’s air traffic control system
Rather than being housed within Transport Canada, the new system would fall under a newly created independent nonprofit called NAV Canada

NAV is funded directly through passenger fees without parliamentary approval, and since it’s not a government entity, it’s exempted from civil service requirements, rigid procurement rules, and other barriers that dogged the old system
In the ’80s and ’90s, Transport had spent $18 million Canadian dollars and six years to modernize its radar system

When NAV undertook a comparable extension in 1997, it completed the project in about six months and at a cost of $6 million. “That whole process of modernizing and bringing new technology to bear on air traffic control,” said Gradek, “has paid out handsomely to the Canadian air traffic control system.” Douglas Mein, a senior director of Transport Canada during the transition, later testified to the British Parliament that moving the air traffic control system to an independent nonprofit freed it from the red tape that often prevented necessary hiring and tied up technological investments for years on end

A few years after NAV took over in 1996, Canada’s air traffic controllers started retiring the paper strips they once used to track flights in favor of an electronic system , an upgrade that the US only started rolling out in 2022 .  Over the decades, Canada’s air traffic control system seems to have become more resilient, while the US has just gotten more vulnerable to disruption as its technology continues to molder
American policymakers have repeatedly pointed to Canada’s success in arguing for a restructuring of America’s air traffic control system

Most recently, under the first Trump administration, Republicans pushed for a Canada-style restructuring that floundered in Congress, seemingly under pressure from the private aviation industry, which was concerned that such an arrangement would prioritize the interests of the commercial airline industry.  Others have pointed to fears that such a system would lead to a loss of public accountability
Some also note that Canada, while seemingly still better off than the US, has run into its own renewed staffing shortages and other air traffic control issues in recent years
But fixing America’s air traffic control system might not necessarily require this kind of privatization

In The Atlantic last year, Dorothy Robyn, who oversaw aviation policy under the Clinton administration — which also pushed for a similar spinoff for the FAA — argued that air traffic control ought to be spun off into a standalone entity, possibly one that would still be governmental
This would, she suggests, contribute to efficiency, while also ensuring the independence of safety regulators, who are currently housed within the FAA itself
Since 1995, Robyn wrote, more than 60 countries have separated their air traffic control system from regulators, some through standalone nonprofits but others through government entities

For example, Germany and New Zealand both migrated their air traffic control systems away from their transportation departments and into government-run entities that are still publicly owned, but have much more freedom to hire workers and spend passenger fees on improvements than the FAA does

Even if the US is not destined for Canadian-style independent air traffic control, a reform that allows the FAA to tap into the fees we all pay on our flights without having to grovel to Congress could help the institution better plan and invest in its technology and staff in the long run

A more fluid and regularized funding scheme would hardly fix everything overnight, but it would at least present a vision for the future of the nation’s air traffic control system that neither requires intermittent multibillion-dollar checks nor panic-inducing admonition that without literally any funding right now , the system that keeps Americans safe in the sky is “going to continue to fail,” as Duffy proclaimed on Friday. “There is a way for the system to be able to, in fact, build in redundancy, build in resilience, and build in backups,” said Gradek, but to do so, “air traffic control needs constant funding, needs constant handholding, and you cannot have these battles to figure out where the next dollar is going to come from.”

title: What the midterms taught us
excerpt: Newly elected members of Congress pose for a group photograph on the steps of the US Capitol Building on November 12, 2026, in Washington, DC | Andrew Harnik/Ge
body: Newly elected members of Congress pose for a group photograph on the steps of the US Capitol Building on November 12, 2026, in Washington, DC | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Everyone from party insiders to the pundits have now parsed the results from the midterm elections, and few races are left to call

Soon, the political world will turn its sights to the 2028 presidential election — but first, America, Actually is taking a moment to reflect on eight months of reporting across the country.  That included anger about the construction of a data center in southern New Jersey ; Democratic hopes for a governing trifecta in Wisconsin , understanding the “Trump slump” — a combination of the pain from tariffs and the fear of immigration enforcement — in Las Vegas ; and hearing voters in a crucial swing district in Pennsylvania connect the war in Iran with high gas prices.  No one votes for president in 2027, but the issues that we saw on the road are a reminder that politics doesn’t only live in the voting booth (and, of course, they’ll have implications for 2028)
This week on America, Actually, I spoke with host Astead Herndon about the moments that we just can’t stop thinking about from our reporting

Below is an excerpt from that conversation, focusing on two aspects of this year’s midterms: how the results could reverberate in the GOP presidential race and what Angie Nixon’s close loss in her Senate race in Florida says about who the Democratic Party establishment will choose to support as the 2028 presidential primary gets underway in 2027
It has been edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, including a discussion of Trump’s declining cultural cachet, an evolving Democratic base, and the rise of the lefty boomer resistance
You can listen to full episodes of America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch on Vox’s YouTube channel
We reported that there were really two strategies that Republicans were using going into this year’s midterm
The first one was basically ignore Trump or distance yourself from Trump, and the other one was to throw money at the polling problem

I don’t really want to flatten that analysis too much, but there are plenty of examples of those who had actually distanced themselves from Trump who ended up losing, right? I’m thinking about Mike Lawler from New York
Obviously, Vivek Ramaswamy in his Ohio governor’s race crashed and burned
We’ve had a lot of really high-profile races where going away from Trump didn’t really work
One foot in and one foot out doesn’t help when something is this universally disliked
And also, the Republican Party didn’t use the levers of power at any point to push back against what Trump has been doing in the last couple years
Like, it was time to shine and to say something, and they didn’t
But what does that mean for 2027? Is the Trump era over? I don’t like that question because at the same time, we’ve seen him use executive power
I don’t think he’s going to back off of his agenda
Steven Miller’s the new chief of staff
Obviously, that represents a double down in itself
But it’s up to Congress to do its job to reassert itself, right? Which they have abdicated completely
Yeah, they’ve abdicated on their own
And so I think it remains to be seen how they even go about the work of holding [Trump] accountable
The other piece is that Trump remains the most popular figure within the Republican Party
And the one thing we know about Republicans is that they circle around him as he’s embattled
And so I just don’t think we can assume that even a mass rejection from the public now means he does not have the most important role in choosing their nominee for the future
I think that’s going to be a big question that 2027 plays out
His popularity specifically with them is intact
Does that change? Do you think that the distancing or playing the blame game that we’re seeing from Vice President JD Vance or Florida Gov
Ron DeSantis, does that signal anything for 2027, or it’s too early? It means that Vance has some challengers
It means DeSantis is probably running, and Ted Cruz and all these others
And I do think that that coronation that might have seemed like a cakewalk three weeks ago is less so now
But I think we’ve got some more twists and turns to come

My last one, honestly, is an answer I’ve thought about a lot when we talked to Angie Nixon , the Senate Democratic candidate in Florida, and it was actually when I asked her about her joining the Democratic Socialists of America, that became such a way that national politics was defining her race

And one of the things I remember is the way that she shrugged off the idea that she should be defined by that label. and I think it really came through in that interview that this was someone who had their own political brand, that was kind of marching to the beat of their own drum, and that was what drove that primary win in Florida

I think this matters a lot for 2027: The gap between how national politics and our kind of media ecosystem sees these fights, particularly between moderate, progressive, DSA, the center, is not how the country’s engaging

The fuzziness is so important, and I think a candidate like that — who now data’s telling us won counties like Miami-Dade [in Florida] — I think speaks to the idea that people are ingesting individuals and their ideas rather than the labels that sometimes we put them in

The other thing I was thinking about when thinking about Angie Nixon — obviously there’s been a huge discussion about whether the Democratic Party missed a chance to invest in her race and win in Florida
I think we’re entering a period where those types of insiders’ decisions matter a lot
When we talk about the 2027 presidential race, there’ll be no primaries decided
This will be a lot of community group endorsements and access, handshaking, and stuff like that

title: Donald Trump loves Jensen Huang. Everyone else…
excerpt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Nvidia/Japan AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo on July 16, 2026. | Philip Fong/AFP via Getty Images Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the Nvidia/Japan AI Ecosystem Reception in Tokyo on July 16, 2026. | Philip Fong/AFP via Getty Images Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company

But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world
And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution

Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies
That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution
His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful

Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president
This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum
It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment , who want to win an AI race against China
It includes economic populists in both parties, who resent China’s economic sway
It even includes some leading members of the Trump administration itself — Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have reportedly pushed for tighter chip restrictions
It also contains some even odder bedfellows
The coalition includes people who want to slow down the AI race, like the tech safety advocates who warn that advanced AI could cause human extinction

Yet it also includes two major US frontier AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic , who hope to impede the growth of Chinese competitors by limiting their access to chips.  All of these disparate groups come together around the core idea that the US urgently needs to do more to stop advanced chips from getting to China
Selling AI chips to China is like “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said
Standing against them all — and often getting his way with Trump — has been Jensen Huang

Beyond the obvious — Nvidia’s business is selling chips, and Huang wants to be able to sell more chips in more places — Huang is associated with a camp in the AI policy debate that some have dubbed with “let it rip.” Along with former White House AI czar David Sacks , Huang has scoffed at warnings that AI could cause human extinction, calling them “irresponsible” and “doomsday narratives.” He’s also dismissed some national security concerns, saying that being a “China hawk” was a “badge of shame” and said that the bigger risk to American influence over AI would be US companies losing market share around the world

So Huang’s ouster and the claims of Chinese espionage around it have opened up an opportunity for a shakeup in US policy — and a rare chance for those China hawks to potentially investigate, undermine, and push out their rivals, while seizing the policy reins around chip exports.  Trump administration officials who want tougher restrictions have their knives out for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a frequent ally of Huang’s
There’s a bipartisan push in Congress for new export controls legislation before the end of the year
Congressional Republican committee chairs are demanding Huang and Lutnick come in and testify in the coming weeks , before Democrats take over Congress
Plus, there are the partisan incentives for Democrats to dig into the question of what Trump knew about all this (he was reportedly briefed on the spy concerns last fall )

And there are political incentives for ambitious Republicans to find an issue on which they can distance themselves from an unpopular administration without antagonizing their conservative base.  With so many different forces invested in the outcome, you can bet this topic will continue to dominate headlines for months to come — with unpredictable results for both the new Democratic Congress, the future of the GOP, and the AI boom

The many critics of Jensen Huang’s influence on the Trump administration In Washington itself, the most influential faction opposed to Huang is the bipartisan national security establishment, most of whom strongly believe in the necessity of competing with China for global influence.  These “ China hawks ” were influential in the Biden administration and have historically been dominant in GOP administrations and on GOP-controlled congressional committees

And many of them have been flabbergasted at Trump’s policies toward China and Chips this term. “I don’t think we should be using any American technology to uplift China’s capabilities in AI given how era-defining this technology will be in national security and in our economy,” Vivek Chilukuri of the Center for a New American Security, a center-left think tank, told me. “A company’s going to argue for this, that’s what companies do
But the interest of any one company should not be trumping the national security of the United States
Moving further right, there’s a MAGA-aligned faction that is skeptical of foreign wars such as Trump’s conflict in Iran — but even some of them are still quite antagonistic to China
Take, for instance, Trump’s onetime campaign manager and White House adviser Steve Bannon

He’s been furiously protesting Huang’s influence on the administration for more than a year — in September 2025, he argued that Huang should be arrested for being “an agent of influence of the Chinese Communist Party,” and argued we needed to “shut down” China’s “access to technology, chips, and training.” Advocates and politicians focused on economic issues and reining in corporate power also have long criticized Nvidia

Oren Cass of the center-right group American Compass wrote an article titled “Break up Nvidia” last year, arguing that “its excessive concentration of power is exactly what antitrust law intends to combat.”  Meanwhile, the left, Sen
Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), a longtime critic of Big Tech, has frequently suggested Huang was corruptly influencing the Trump administration

At a hearing in June, she mentioned that Huang or his company had donated to Trump’s inauguration and his White House ballroom project. “If it’s not plain old-fashioned bribery, it sure smells like it,” she said
Many in the AI safety advocacy world have also long criticized — and feared — Nvidia
That’s in part because they hope slowing down sales of AI chips abroad could slow what they view as a dangerous race to superintelligence

Additionally, after AI safety fears hit the mainstream in September due to Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation and viral warnings, Huang took an increasingly public role in dismissing such fears

Other AI safety advocates cite the company as having a chilling effect on public debate. “For months now, I’ve heard about widespread fear among think tank researchers and policy experts who publish work against Nvidia’s interests,” AI safety researcher Steven Adler wrote last year . “If you speak with people in-the-know at AI companies, fear of retaliation from Nvidia is a major concern when staking out policy positions.” Indeed, OpenAI and Anthropic are highly dependent on Nvidia for its chips, so open criticism of the company is not common

Yet those big two US AI labs have been at odds with Nvidia in urging the Trump administration to do more to crack down on Chinese access to advanced chips, and to more heavily scrutinize Chinese “open source” AI models
But to Huang and others in his camp, the growth of Chinese AI is a feature, not a bug

Sacks, for instance, has repeatedly argued that “open weight” or “open source” models — which make their parameters publicly available, in contrast to the proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic — would help avert “an unsafe and dystopian future where advanced AI capabilities are centralized and controlled by only a few hands.” The leading open weight models are currently from Chinese companies

Huang has also used a more straightforward argument: that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States of America. “American technology has to win across the world at every single layer,” he said in May . “If we can export chips, we should.” Now it will be left to Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, to carry that message, instead of a rock-star founder with a global cult following that’s drawn comparisons to Steve Jobs at his peak at Apple
Her first task: taking stock of all the powerful actors across the political, advocacy, and business world rooting for her to fail

title: Being single can be a gift. Here’s how to embrace it.
excerpt: When you’re single, it’s hard to avoid questions about your dating life. “Are you seeing anyone?” people will ask. “Had any fun dates?”  Well-meant as it m
body: When you’re single, it’s hard to avoid questions about your dating life. “Are you seeing anyone?” people will ask. “Had any fun dates?”  Well-meant as it may be, these questions can leave you feeling less than, like you’ve failed in something that you were supposed to have figured out by now
At their worst, frequent questions about your love life imply that you don’t have love at all
Because we all learn, sooner or later, that there’s an expected direction of travel in life: Get an education; then a job
And, of course, if you tick all those boxes, the expectation is that you’ll live happily ever after.  Our rational brains understand this is just a fairy tale

But the gravitational pull of its mythic expectations can feel impossible to withstand — hence those questions as you catch up with friends at happy hour or pass the cranberry sauce during the holidays
And it isn’t just social pressure; there are numerous policies and tax breaks that incentivize marriage and children

The architecture of our society is built for couples, so if you’re single — whether by choice or by circumstance — how should you live?  Who better to ask than a nun?  Anne Curtis is a Sister of Mercy and the executive director of Mercy by the Sea , a retreat center in Madison, Connecticut

As a young woman, she made a vow to dedicate her life to God, which meant remaining single; it didn’t mean withdrawing from love — but allowing for more of it.  If you’re imagining a stern old lady dressed in a habit, let me quickly disabuse you of that notion
For starters, Curtis, like most American nuns today, wears regular clothes
And she’s spent her life putting love for others into action

She campaigned for a living wage, affordable housing, and environmental protections through Network , a Catholic social justice lobbying group, and represented American nuns during a period of highly publicized tension with the more conservative Vatican.  In her, I see a model of singlehood that challenges the assumptions many of us have about being unpartnered, and the pervasive idea that coupledom equals love and singledom equals loneliness
First, Curtis has lived and worked among her community of sisters since entering the novitiate decades ago, building deep friendships

Second, without a partner, Curtis has been able to offer much more love to her family and friends, especially in times of trial. “One of my sisters lost her spouse three years ago, and to this day, we check in every single day,” she says. “Just a really quick text
It’s part of, for me, entering into the day…
I sit in quiet, I pray, I walk the land here, I text my sister

I have a whole list of people who I specifically remember each day in my own prayer and reflection, because of something they’ve asked or some need they have.” When I ask if she gives more love than she receives, Curtis challenges the assumptions of the question: “The more that I’ve understood and come in touch with the fact that I was created and came out of love, then I’m also able to offer that love [to others]
And it’s responded to.” The work of her faith is to ground herself in that reality. “The more genuine and authentic I am, the more love I experience,” she says

This experience of belovedness enables Curtis to carry an awareness of, and tend to, the larger needs of the world. “I stand at the threshold of the land and the water and the sky,” she says. “I’m so aware of the expanse of the universe all around me and the worlds of Palestine, Ukraine, Sudan, Ethiopia
So many places where there’s incredible turmoil

And, I feel like, because of my life, I belong to a worldwide family.” Of course, her life isn’t always easy. “When we say yes to something, we say no to a whole lot of other things,” she says. “It would be a lie to say I never felt the loneliness of my life choice or to say ‘I wonder what my life would have been like if…’” Particularly in her younger years, she found it difficult

But, with time, she realized this yearning was just part of the process — and it was wise to embrace what she had in all its joys and its struggles. “At some point in your life, it’s important to say yes to something,” she says
James Martin understands this equally well
He’s a Jesuit priest and editor-at-large of America magazine
Similar to Curtis, he, too, took a vow of chastity and has therefore lived as a single person, a journey he documents in his memoir Work in Progress

Although he affirms that the Catholic Church actively promotes marriage, the “more basic is the idea that we’re meant for love.” Think about that: Humans are designed for connection — and the way that love is given and received is different for each person, Martin says

Whether you find that in a partnership, in a community, in a family, or in service, what matters, according to this Catholic tradition, is that we love and are loved in return.  Should anyone doubt that, Martin laughs and says, “Let me just remind you…Jesus was single!”  “God calls us to be who we are,” Martin says. “You are called to be yourself in all of your beauty.” The question to ask, he says, is “How can I live out that calling in a loving way, and in a fruitful way and in a way that will help me to — one of my favorite words from Thomas Aquinas — help me to flourish?”  Martin does this in his own life via the Daily Examen
The Examen is a roughly 500-year-old prayer practice developed by the founder of the Jesuit order, St
At the end of a day, maybe as you lay down to sleep, you go through your day hour by hour to notice the presence of God

If the word God gets in your way, try asking yourself, “Where did I notice love today?” It might be in the smile exchanged with a baby in the grocery aisle, while planning a friend’s birthday dinner, or getting a hug from your mom
If you’ve never tried it before, give it a go
It’s a powerful practice of gratitude and trains you to notice the beauty in your life
In my experience, the Examen helps me practice what Martin describes as having what you have, rather than focusing on what you don’t.  Naturally, that shift can take time

Brianna Cayo Cotter, a social impact executive in her 40s who is single, has noticed this change over decades, too. “In my 20s, I was dating lots of different people,” she says, “figuring out…heartbreak and highs and lows.” Then, in her 30s, she felt a longing and a yearning as she saw a lot of people coupling off. “And that felt…like a loss at the time.” But now she’s come to a great acceptance — partly because she’s seen that marriage is no guarantee to stave off loneliness, and comes with many of its own burdens. “I think my life is actually better and more rich and has more love and companionship in it than most of the couples that I know,” she says. “Not all! But, really most.” So many coupled friends struggle to build community in their forties, for example. “I can empathize, but I cannot relate at all.”  But more than this, being single gives Cayo Cotter more time. “More time in your life to be juicy and spread more love and deepen it and have profoundly intimate relationships with lots of different people in different ways.” Whether she’s traveling with others, hosting friends, or getting together with neighbors on her block, Cayo Cotter lives a life in which she is wildly loved.  Of course, she still gets those questions. “I remember my mom, when she was visiting me one time, she was like, ‘But who would go and pick you up when you get your colonoscopy?’” Cayo Cotter says with a laugh. “I was like, ‘I could ask 20 people to do that!’” Because she gives love so generously, she receives it bountifully, too.  And despite not being a nun, or even religiously affiliated, this practice of loving and being loved has a spiritual quality for Cayo Cotter
She practices yoga daily, and says one closing prayer really resonates with her: “ The light in me sees the light in you

And the more that you can go out into the world with a greater light shining from you… that is how to live.” Curtis would agree: “Whatever your faith dimension is or practice or belief, I think they all, in some way, are a call to love. … There’s limitless ways to offer love and be loved.”  So when people ask whether you’re dating anyone, you might want to answer the bigger question that they’re prodding for: “No, I’m not partnered

title: Democrats could raise the minimum wage next year. How high should they go?
excerpt: A decade after the Democratic Party rallied around the Fight for 15 movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economi
body: A decade after the Democratic Party rallied around the Fight for 15 movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economic question for the new majority. | Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images In the wake of the midterm elections in which Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate , a growing number of politicians and activists have begun calling, publicly and privately, for Congress to seize the moment and pass the first federal minimum wage increase in 17 years.  After running campaigns centered on the cost of living, Democrats and their allies say raising the $7.25 federal minimum closer to a “living wage” — i.e., enough for a full-time worker to cover basics like rent, food, and healthcare — is the obvious next step for their affordability mandate

A minimum wage increase also has a political advantage because businesses, not the government, cover the cost, meaning it has little effect on the deficit and doesn’t compete with other priorities for federal dollars. “I’ve been talking with a lot of different Democrats on the Hill and they’ve been calling it a first 100-day issue,” said Jared Bernstein, who chaired President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers and is now at the liberal Center for American Progress.  Rahm Emanuel, who is widely expected to run for president in 2028, has been urging Democrats to act , and it was a top issue for the party when he ran its campaign arm in 2006. “Pass a minimum wage $20 by 2030,” he said on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast after the election

Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has also been making media rounds calling for raising the wage to “at least $20 bucks an hour.” On Thursday, Hakeem Jeffries, who’s expected to be the House speaker, identified raising the wage as a priority, but ducked press questions about specifics
Key takeaways Many Democrats want to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to about $20 an hour by 2030
Most research finds past increases raised pay without costing many jobs
But few places have set a minimum that high relative to local wages, so economists don’t know where the limit is
Critics warn a high national minimum could hurt lower-wage states the most and lead employers to raise prices or cut hours, benefits, and training
Raising the minimum wage is popular across party lines, and because the cost falls on businesses and their customers rather than taxpayers, it adds little to the federal deficit

A decade after the party rallied around the “Fight for 15” movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economic question for the new Democratic majority, as well as in states where they have new governing trifectas

Josh Shapiro has pledged to sign a $15 minimum wage bill , while in Wisconsin, Gov.-elect David Crowley has targeted a gradual increase to $20 .  In recent years, a wave of research built on the 30 states that raised their own minimums has convinced many economists that modest increases cost few, if any, jobs

That evidence, plus voters’ anger about the cost of living, has rallied progressive experts around a new federal benchmark equal to two-thirds of the hourly median wage, or roughly $20 by 2030.  But that threshold is also near the upper end of what researchers have actually studied, and even economists who support it acknowledge that no one knows how high the minimum wage can go before it starts costing a significant number of jobs or increasing prices at a time when inflation is a major concern
Skeptics warn that a national minimum that high could hit the country’s lowest-wage places hardest, just as AI introduces new threats to the jobs young and less-experienced workers depend on
Still, raising the minimum wage is popular with voters, and even some Republicans have expressed openness to cutting a deal. “You want to raise the minimum wage? I’m for that,” Sen
Josh Hawley (R-MO) told reporters last week
The last wage increase was signed by a Republican president after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the 2006 midterms, much as they did this month

Trump, who has previously called the $7.25 minimum wage “ a very low number ” recently told Politico he doesn’t want to “just be sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” Some Democrats want to go even further, like Sen
Chris Murphy of Connecticut, whose bill introduced over the summer would require big companies to pay $25 within about five years and smaller ones by the late 2030s

Murphy makes the case for his bill less on labor-market research and more on economic fairness. “It’s not like we can’t pay a $25 minimum wage,” Murphy said after announcing his legislation. “We just choose not to.” And in New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani ran on a $30 minimum wage by 2030 , though the plan hasn’t gotten traction in the state legislature, which would have to approve it
As Democrats look to act in 2027 and beyond, the empirical debate over how high the minimum wage can safely go is getting entangled with the populist one over how high the party should aim

These debates are especially important because the party may have far more power to raise wages than they expected before their midterm wins, both in Congress and in states and cities around the country
While previous efforts in Congress have been stymied by procedural barriers, Senate Democrats are now within reach of a filibuster-proof majority as soon as 2029

Far from a messaging exercise, the question of how high wages should be at the bottom is now a live policy issue that the party needs to take seriously — with potentially severe consequences if they misstep

How Democrats work through these tensions will shape both how much low-wage workers might gain, and what they might lose, and how much of the party’s answer to the cost of living rests on the minimum wage at all
From $15 to $20 (and beyond) Beginning in 2012 and backed by the Service Employees International Union, fast-food workers walked off their jobs, demanding $15 an hour and the right to form a union

The Fight for 15 became a national movement, spreading to other sectors like academia, airports, and childcare, and it pushed past the position of President Barack Obama and congressional Democrats, who were calling then for a $10.10 minimum
In 2015, congressional Democrats introduced the Raise the Wage Act, which would have increased the federal minimum wage to $12 an hour by 2020
Hillary Clinton campaigned on a $12 minimum in the 2016 primary, while Sanders leaned into the $15 standard

By the time the general election rolled around, even with Clinton as the nominee, the Democratic Party platform had embraced $15, and by 2017, Democrats, now with Sanders as the Senate’s lead sponsor, updated the Raise the Wage Act to a $15 target
The House passed the $15 bill in 2019, but it died in the Republican-controlled Senate

In 2021, the Senate parliamentarian blocked Democrats from adding it to Biden’s pandemic relief package, though it’s possible a future Congress might feature a different parliamentarian with a different perspective
Bobby Scott raised the bill’s target again, this time to $17 an hour
But while progress in Washington stalled, leaders around the country took action
Since 2014, 28 states and Washington, DC, have passed laws raising their minimum wages, and nearly 70 cities and counties now have minimums higher than their state’s
Some of the increases came through legislation, while others came from ballot measure campaigns, including in red states like Arkansas, Florida, Missouri, and Nebraska
Eighteen states and DC now have minimums of $15 or more
Though raising the minimum wage has long drawn support across party lines, in June, Oklahoma voters decisively rejected a measure that would have raised the state’s minimum from $7.25 to $15 by 2029

Opponents argued that the raise , plus automatic yearly increases tied to inflation, would have driven up prices and hurt small businesses. (The vote also came during a low-turnout June primary , when only about a quarter of registered voters cast ballots.) That same month, Murphy introduced the Living Wage for All Act , outflanking Sanders’s Raise the Wage Act from the left
Murphy, who is also widely expected to run for president, has argued that Democrats should lean harder into economic populism to win back the working class

A $25 minimum wage is “the bare minimum of what workers deserve — and of what workers should expect from their leaders,” he declared in an essay accompanying his bill’s release. “It’s also what’s best for the health of our economy and country.” Murphy and Sanders discussed the Living Wage for All Act earlier this year, a Murphy spokesperson told me, adding that “conversations among the caucus are ongoing as to how best raise the minimum wage across the nation.” What the research says A generation ago, efforts to boost the minimum wage ran into a recurring problem: a widespread consensus among economists that increases came with serious trade-offs, like fewer jobs and higher prices

And not just free-market conservatives, but more liberal economists like former New York Times columnist Paul Krugman, who in 1998 chastised activists who believed wages “can be set based on considerations of justice, not supply and demand, without unpleasant side effects.” But that consensus quietly shifted over the years as more states and cities experimented with ambitious wage increases — and ran into fewer difficulties than expected

title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
excerpt: Brain implant volunteers want more respect: Ian Burkhart, who had a brain implant for seven-and-a-half years, helped develop new guidelines pushing for trial pa
body: Brain implant volunteers want more respect: Ian Burkhart, who had a brain implant for seven-and-a-half years, helped develop new guidelines pushing for trial participants to have the option to be recognized as genuine research collaborators and listed as coauthors on scientific papers

Your brain data should be yours: The guidelines argue that participants' neural data is personal information, and that NDAs or embargoes should not block someone from sharing their own brain data with their doctor
Losing an implant can feel like losing a limb: When funding dried up or companies collapsed, participants like Burkhart lost devices—and abilities—with little warning

The guidelines call for researchers to fund and plan removals carefully, giving participants real time to prepare " data-chronoton-post-id="1148474" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades

Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014
He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs)
Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist

But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old
Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control
He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement
The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head
Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it
The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers
Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences
The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy
The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories
One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants

During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t
He says he was a key member of the research team
Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says
Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.   The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy

That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention
In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants
Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data
Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data
Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement

But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.  The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors. “It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.” The guidelines also address what comes after a trial
Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding

When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.) Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp
But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again
Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant
When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights
Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines
Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it
And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that
Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards
They don’t all spell out explicit solutions
They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low
The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time

body: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory
